This guide compares a day on the phone with a day on the platform side by side, and gives you checklists for the profile, availability and route settings worth sorting out before your first search.

Why does finding loads by phone still take hours?

When you're the dispatcher, the bookkeeper and the drivers' boss all at once, searching by phone eats the hours: you ring brokers one by one, listen to prices, jot jobs down on a scrap of paper and hope someone rings back. The same empty leg you could fill in ten minutes takes half a day.

The hidden costs of phone-based searching in a 1–12 lorry firm

The hidden costs aren't the per-minute call charges but the interrupted work: every call breaks off invoicing, checking CMR consignment notes or planning the next job. The note on a scrap of paper saying "who pays and when" gets forgotten precisely when you need the money most.

In a three-lorry business, a single dispatch run can mean 15–20 calls a day just to fill empty legs. Each call lasts three to five minutes on average, but the real cost is the context switch: when you go back to invoicing after a call, it takes fifteen minutes to get back up to speed. Ten calls a day in practice means an hour and a half of fragmented working time that vanishes from the diary without anyone noticing.

In a one-person business it's worse: when you're driving yourself and making calls during breaks, searching by phone eats into driving time. A break that should be a rest turns into a stressful round of calls with uncertain results. Voicemail is the most common answer, and leaving a call-back request means waiting around, which only adds to fatigue.

Freight exchanges are built for exactly this: Teleroute describes how its service works as shippers publishing loads and hauliers finding them using search criteria, with no phone call (Teleroute). RAHTIS starts from the same problem at the smaller end: you publish the job once and follow it step by step (RAHTIS – Veokorraldus ja veobörs).

How does a freight exchange find a load for your lorry?

A freight exchange works as a two-way marketplace: shippers publish loads, and hauliers find them with filters or by posting their own empty legs. The system matches the two sides automatically when the details fit. The same logic applies in RAHTIS (RAHTIS – Transportledning och lastbörs): a published load is visible to those searching, and you follow the job step by step.

Search filters: origin, destination, date and vehicle type

The search is based on four fields. Origin and destination define your route, the date tells when the lorry is free, and the vehicle type (refrigerated, trailer, container chassis) weeds out loads your vehicle isn't suited to. The more precisely these are filled in on your profile, the fewer matches you get that you have to turn down.

In practice the chain of filters works like this: first you choose the origin area, for example "Helsinki + 150 km". Then you add a destination filter, such as "Tampere or Turku". The third filter is the date: "loading Monday morning, delivery Tuesday". The fourth is the vehicle type: "semi-trailer, 13.6 metres, tail lift". The system only shows the loads that pass all four filters. If you leave one field empty, you get dozens of matches that don't suit your vehicle, and you waste time scrolling through them.

Posting an offer vs searching actively

In an active search you browse the loads on offer yourself and submit quotes. By posting your empty leg, you tell the other side where you're heading and when, and the load can come to you. In practice the two complement each other: searching fills the lorry today, and a posted empty leg finds the return load for tomorrow.

What information do you need to prepare before you start searching for loads online?

An exchange search only works first time if your profile, vehicle details and route settings are in order before you open your first request for quotation. An incomplete profile shows up as a bidder nobody picks.

Profile checklist

  • Company details: business ID (Y-tunnus), VAT number, insurance and CMR liability details
  • Vehicles: lorries, trailers, payload, lifting equipment, number of lashing straps
  • Drivers: licence categories, ADR qualification, languages spoken
  • Payment terms and invoicing details ready in advance, so they aren't up for negotiation on every job

Many exchanges show the other party's credit rating and reviews before you quote. Trans.eu's documentation covers, among other things, members' ratings and payment history (Trans.eu Help Center). It's worth gathering the same information about your own customers: in RAHTIS (RAHTIS – Kuljetusten hallinta ja rahtipörssi) you can track not only the job status but also who pays what.

Availability and route settings checklist

SettingWhat to prepare
Origin areasHome town + 100–200 km radius
Empty-leg daysCalendar for the next 2 weeks
Route preferencesAreas to avoid, your preferred routes
Return load conditionsMinimum rate, maximum length, unloading time
Vehicle availabilityFree lorry + trailer, loading time
Pricing guidelinesMinimum rate per km, separate surcharges

Once these are filled in, a quote is a click, not a phone call.

A day on the phone vs a day on the platform: the dispatch workflow side by side

Morning: finding loads and quoting

On a phone day, the morning goes on calls: nobody can see who has loads on offer, so the enquiries go one after another. On a platform day, you open the freight exchange, filter routes and loading times, and see the available loads at a glance. Submitting a quote takes a couple of clicks, and the reply arrives as a notification without the phone ringing while you're driving.

Daytime: confirmations, consignment note, driver details

This is where the difference is greatest. In the phone model, the booking, load details and consignment note files live in different places: text messages, email and a scrap of paper. On a platform, the same job appears as a single whole: the driver sees the addresses, times and consignment note directly on their phone, and you follow the status without ringing to ask "where are you?".

When loads, drivers and documents are in the same system, dispatch shifts from chasing information to making decisions: you choose the next load, and the system passes the information on. In RAHTIS, the consignment note, confirmation and status tracking sit in the same view, so in a four-lorry business you no longer leaf through scraps of paper to see who pays and what's still open. RAHTIS doesn't pull loads from other exchanges, but you can enter your own customers' jobs, including ones agreed elsewhere, in the same system alongside jobs from RAHTIS's own offer desk. The Latvian-language RAHTIS page (RAHTIS – Transporta vadība un kravu birža) explains how your own customers and offer-desk jobs are handled in one place. An honest note: if there aren't enough loads on the platform for a particular route, you'll still have to make calls or check another exchange, so the phone won't disappear entirely.

Evening: invoicing and payment tracking

On a phone day, the evening goes on matching consignment notes with quote notes to raise invoices. On a platform, the end of a job prompts for the POD, and the invoice goes out from the same chain. Payment tracking is visible in the system, so you no longer need a "who owes what" list in a paper notebook.

What are the risks of giving up the phone, and how do you vet the other party?

A phone call is the traditional way to "sniff out" whether a client is reliable, but systematic checks can replace it: online, a fraudster leaves a trail, as long as you note the details down before accepting the job.

Counterparty checklist

Before accepting a load from a freight exchange, check at least: the company's official name and business ID, the client's contact details on a company email address (not a Gmail address), payment history from the exchange's rating points, and whether the client is a verified member. Trans.eu and TIMOCOM both offer members' credit ratings and payment behaviour data for exactly this purpose (Trans.eu credit information service). Keep the list and fill it in for every new client, even if the load is urgent.

Payment terms and advance payments

The biggest risk isn't a wrong address but money: is payment at 30 days or 60, and who pays if the goods arrive but the invoice isn't paid? Agree payment terms in writing before loading, and beware of cash-in-advance requests, which are a common scam. In RAHTIS, the job details, consignment note and invoicing run through the same step-by-step view, so the agreement and documents stay paired (RAHTIS – Transportmanagement und Frachtenbörse).

When is the phone still the better option, even if you use a freight exchange?

The phone beats the platform when time is short. If the lorry is standing empty and a load has to be found within the hour, a direct call to a shipper you know or to other hauliers working the area is often the fastest way to get a load moving.

The second situation is an urgent or unusual load. If the loading changes mid-day, a trailer is missing or the delivery time falls through, it's sorted on the phone in seconds. Writing a message and waiting for a reply takes the same minutes.

The third reason is relationships. Your regular customers and most important shippers are used to hearing from you, and direct contact maintains trust when jobs from the freight exchange alone aren't enough to fill the week.

So in practice: the exchange handles searching and paperwork, the phone handles urgency and relationships.

How do you start searching for loads digitally when you have no history on the platform yet?

A new account is a blank sheet, but the first job comes sooner if your profile doesn't look anonymous. Fill in your company details, registration numbers, number of drivers and insurance details straight away, and upload a sample CMR or two from previous deliveries. Respond to your first quotes within a few minutes: on platforms, response time is visible to the other side, and a quick acknowledgement makes up for a missing review history.

Start with small jobs in your local area, even if the margin is thin. The first successful jobs earn the reviews that open up better-paid routes. Be as careful as you would on the phone: confirm the loading time in writing, ask for a signed consignment note and send the POD straight away.

In small hauliers' experience, it's precisely this combination, load search, POD and invoicing in the same workflow, that makes the switch worthwhile once the paper notebook and separate logins start to become a burden (Reddit discussion of a small haulier's TMS experience).

Which tools for a small haulage business: exchanges and TMS in one package?

For a small business, tools fall into two camps: freight exchanges such as Trans.eu, TIMOCOM and Teleroute handle finding loads and filling empty trucks, while a TMS handles dispatch, consignment notes and invoicing. Many run them side by side: the exchange login in one window, a scrap of paper in another, email in a third.

What RAHTIS is suited to and where it falls short

RAHTIS combines both: it is a TMS with its own offer desk, where the shipper publishes the job once and follows the work step by step, while the haulier fills empty legs and keeps the whole fleet in one place. It does not merge loads from other exchanges. It works from a single lorry upwards, and the notebook and carrying paper CMRs back to the office are replaced by a workflow found in a single view.

To be honest, RAHTIS doesn't solve everything. It doesn't replace accounting software or a bank connection, and it doesn't show loads from other exchanges. If you need a wide international load supply or advanced reporting for a larger fleet, a traditional exchange and a bigger TMS may suit you better. RAHTIS is designed for one to twelve lorries.

FAQ

Is using a freight exchange chargeable for a small firm, and how does pricing usually work?

Most exchanges charge a monthly or annual subscription that varies with membership size and features. Some charge separately for each confirmed job. Compare pricing based on your own volumes: for one to three lorries a lighter subscription is often enough, and trial periods help you test whether searching pays off before you commit.

Can I combine several exchanges (e.g. Teleroute, TIMOCOM, Trans.eu) into one search without separate logins?

Usually not directly: the exchanges are separate systems, each with its own login and its own filters. In practice, small hauliers keep one or two exchanges open side by side and enter the agreed jobs in a TMS, where they appear in one view. RAHTIS doesn't connect external exchanges, but in it your own customers' jobs and jobs from RAHTIS's own offer desk run under the same workflow.

How is the CMR consignment note handled when the load comes through an exchange?

The consignment note details come with the job information, but signing still takes place at the loading and delivery points. In digital workflows, the driver photographs the signed CMR on a phone and sends the POD to the system immediately after delivery. The paper CMR is still the most common; a fully electronic e-CMR is valid only for carriage between countries that have joined the e-CMR protocol. The most important thing is that the consignment note and the other job details stay in the same chain.

How quickly are loads usually found once a listing is published on the platform?

On popular routes with standard vehicles, offers start coming in within hours, sometimes minutes. With a less common vehicle type or in a remote area, a listing may go days without a match. The quality of the listing directly affects the result: precise availability times, route and vehicle details produce matches faster than a vague listing nobody dares take on.

Do I need a separate TMS, or is a freight exchange account enough?

It depends on how much other work falls outside the exchange. An exchange account handles finding loads, but dispatch, consignment notes, payment tracking and invoicing remain separate tasks. If you run one to twelve lorries and want jobs, documents and invoicing in one view, a TMS adds value. For occasional work with a single lorry, an exchange account may be enough to start with.

kuormituksen-vahentaminen-sahkolasku.title: Reducing peak load: how to cut your electricity bill
kuormituksen-vahentaminen-sahkolasku.description: Smoothing out load peaks cuts the demand charge, if your network tariff has one. How to spot peaks in your consumption data and stage the measures.
kuormituksen-vahentaminen-sahkolasku.html:
Key takeaways

  • If your electricity network (distribution) tariff includes a demand charge, what lowers the bill is smoothing out peak power, not just reducing total consumption; first check your network contract to see whether you have a demand charge and how it is calculated.
  • Depending on the distribution network operator, the demand charge is based on, for example, the month's highest hourly power or the highest power over the past 12 months, in which case a single peak can affect your bill for a whole year.
  • You can get your own consumption data from Fingrid's Datahub customer portal or your network operator's online service, and the peaks can be found in it without a separate meter.
  • Stage the measures in three tiers: free scheduling changes, small control investments and only then larger purchases.
  • You can set timers yourself, but electrical installation work and changes to the grid connection are for an electrical contractor registered with Tukes (the Finnish Safety and Chemicals Agency) and for the network operator.

Reducing peak load means smoothing out peaks in electricity consumption: the same work gets done, but high-power equipment does not all run at once. This guide shows you how to identify peaks in your own consumption data and stage the measures by cost impact and effort, whether it is a warehouse, a workshop or a depot building.

What does reducing peak load mean in practice?

Reducing peak load does not mean driving less or heating the building less. The aim is to smooth out the peaks: to move consumption away from the hours when several high-power appliances run at the same time and push up the demand charge.

Energy and power are different things

Energy (kWh) is what you consume in total. Power (kW) is how much electricity is being used at any one moment. When heating, the compressor, the pressure washer and chargers all run at once, power rises and the meter records a peak. Think of a water supply: energy is the water used over the whole day, power is how many taps are open at the same time. If every tap is opened at once, the flow rate goes up, even though the day's total volume of water stays the same.

Why the peak, not total consumption, is what counts

Not all network tariffs have a demand charge: small connections often pay only a standing charge and an energy-based distribution charge. In demand-based tariffs, used particularly for larger business connections, part of the charge is based on the measured peak power. The basis of calculation varies between network operators: for example, Elenia's price list for large customers uses the month's highest 60-minute average power, while Kuopion Sähköverkko's low-voltage demand tariff uses the highest average hourly power over the past 12 months. In the latter case, a single unsmoothed peak shows up on the bill for a whole year.

The same idea works in the day-to-day running of a haulage firm: once you can identify the rush peaks, you can stagger the work. More on that at the end of the article.

How do you identify load peaks from your own consumption data?

Peaks are found in your own metering data, not by guesswork. You need hourly or 15-minute consumption data for 12 months, a spreadsheet program and an hour of your time.

Step 1: download consumption data for the past 12 months

In Finland, electricity metering data are stored in Datahub, run by the transmission system operator Fingrid. Log in to the Datahub customer portal (oma.datahub.fi) with Suomi.fi identification (the Finnish public e-identification service), or use the online service of your own network operator, such as Caruna or Elenia, and download the data as a CSV file. Note that times in the Datahub file are in UTC. If the building has its own sub-meter, its data are even more precise.

A full year covers both the winter heating peaks and summer cooling. Check that the timestamps in the file are hourly or 15-minute and that as little data as possible is missing from the period.

Step 2: work out the peak hour and the average power

Sort the data in descending order. The largest single hour is your peak, and the hours around it tell you which appliances start up at the same time. Then calculate the average power for the year. The ratio of peak to average power tells you how much room there is for smoothing.

If, for example, your peak is 25 kW and your average power is 8 kW, the ratio is over three. That means the peak comes from a few hours in which many appliances run at the same time. If you stagger them, the peak can fall noticeably, and the change in the demand charge can be calculated directly.

Step 3: mark the peaks on a calendar and look for recurring patterns

Record when each peak occurs: date, time and day of the week. Recurring patterns matter more than individual peaks, because routines can be changed.

A single peak is rarely a problem. If the peak hour falls every weekday between 15:00 and 17:00, when the wash bay's water heater, the compressor and the chargers all start at once, it is not chance but structure. A routine like that is the easiest to fix: move one appliance an hour later and measure again. Once the peaks are marked on a calendar, a staged plan comes together quickly.

Which appliances put the most load on the grid, and when?

The big electricity users in a small warehouse, workshop or depot are usually easy to identify. A power peak is typically caused by a few appliances that start up at the same time.

ApplianceTypical peak timeLoad
Electric heating, heat pumps, radiatorsWinter mornings 6–9 and afternoons 16–20Often the largest
Workshop air compressorStart of the working day 7–10High, start-up spike
Wash bay and water heaterAfternoon, when the lorries return to the yardMedium
Charging forklifts, machinery and electric vehiclesEvening and early nightHigh, long-lasting
Lighting and building lightsWinter afternoonsLow

Heating and ventilation behind winter peaks

In the Nordic countries, heating is usually the largest adjustable load. Lower the building temperature at night and at weekends, and move the ventilation boost away from the morning peak. Note that if the whole building is quickly heated back up to working temperature in the morning, the heating itself can become a new peak, so start heating early or in stages. If the heat pump runs at full power at 7:00, bring its start forward to 5:00–6:00, when the rest of the load is still low.

Machines and tools behind daytime peaks

The compressor's start-up spike often coincides with heating. The compressor runs hardest when the tank pressure drops and the machine refills it. If several mechanics start using air tools at 8:00, the compressor and the heating push up the peak together. A timed fill before the shift starts moves this spike away from the other appliances' peak.

Charging electric vehicles and machinery

Schedule charging for the night, when other consumption is low. With several charging points, stagger the start times so that the first vehicle starts charging at 22:00, the second at 23:00 and the third at midnight, or use load management that shares the available power between the charging points. Many chargers already support scheduling, so no investment may be needed.

How do you prioritise the measures?

Stage the measures in three tiers: free scheduling changes first, then small control investments and only then larger purchases. Move to the next tier only once the previous one has been done and measured; otherwise you will buy an expensive solution to a problem that a free fix would have solved.

Tier 1: move consumption away from peak hours

Start by scheduling everything that can be done for free or cheaply. The start times of water heaters, dryers and chargers can often be moved using the appliances' own timers. Forklift and machinery charging should be scheduled for the night. Record the measured peak before and after, so you know how much tier 1 achieved. Changing the control of a permanently installed appliance, such as a water heater, is however electrical work that must be done by an electrical contractor.

Tier 2: control and automation

When scheduling is no longer enough, add control. Motion sensors, staggered thermostats and remote-controlled sockets cost tens or hundreds of euros and remove the risk of forgetting – the same idea as in dispatch: whatever repeats every day is worth automating. At the same time, make sure you can see consumption at hourly or 15-minute level, so the effect of each measure can be verified. A plug-in smart socket is only suitable for appliances whose power is within the socket's rating; high-power appliances are controlled with a permanently installed control system.

Tier 3: investments that only pay off if the peak stays high

Larger purchases, such as replacing the heating system or a load management system for charging, only pay off once tiers 1 and 2 have been done and the peak is still high. First work out how many kilowatts the investment would take off the peak, and compare that with the cost of the investment.

An example: tiers 1 and 2 reduced the peak from 20 kW to 12 kW, and a new heating solution would cost €8,000. If it took a further 2 kW off the peak and the demand charge is €3 per kilowatt per month, the saving is €6 a month and the payback period is over a hundred years. So the investment does not pay off because of the demand charge; it can only pay off if it also saves energy.

How does reducing peak load show up on the electricity bill?

The demand charge on the network bill

If your network tariff includes a demand charge, smoothing out the peaks shows up in the demand charge on your network bill. Electricity tax and energy-based charges depend on the kilowatt-hours consumed, so staggering does not affect them. When the saving shows up depends on how the demand charge is calculated: if it is based on the month's highest power, the saving appears on the next bill, but if it is based on the highest power over the past 12 months, the old peak will continue to affect the bill for months. Changes to the connection's main fuses or connection capacity are agreed with the network operator under its connection terms.

How to calculate the saving yourself

Record the peak power (kW) used as the billing basis before and after the changes. Multiply the reduction in power by the demand charge unit price, which you will find in your network operator's price list, and the comparison is done. An example: if peak power falls from 18 kW to 12 kW and the demand charge is €3 per kilowatt per month, the saving is €18 a month, or €216 a year. If the tier 1 and tier 2 measures cost €150, they pay for themselves in about eight months.

When do you need the network operator or an electrical contractor?

Most peak-load reduction can be done yourself: appliance operating times are moved, heating is controlled with existing settings and consumption is tracked from the metering data. You can change when appliances are used, but you cannot carry out electrical installation work.

A professional is needed when it comes to connection capacity, main fuses, metering, the distribution board or fixed installations. If, for example, charging electric lorries requires more power than the existing connection allows, a change to the connection is always agreed with the network operator. Under the Finnish Electrical Safety Act (1135/2016), electrical work may only be carried out by a business that has registered with Tukes and has a qualified electrical work supervisor; a layperson may only do very simple jobs. More information is available on the Tukes website.

The practical dividing line is simple: if the work concerns the connection or the building's electrical installations, contact an electrical contractor. If it concerns when an appliance starts up using its own settings, you can do it yourself and record the result. For example, scheduling a plug-in appliance with a smart socket is your own measure, but upgrading the main fuses from, say, 25 amps to 35 amps so that more charging points can run at once requires a decision on the connection by the network operator and work by an electrical contractor.

How can the same peak management be applied more widely in a haulage firm?

Peak hours in dispatch too

The same measure–identify–stagger model works for the work itself. Record what time of day the phone rings most: typically in the morning before departures and in the afternoon before planning the next day. These are your firm's load peaks, and they take time away from actual dispatch and invoicing.

Once the peaks are on paper, you can stage the measures: first the recurring questions (sign-off, transport order, payment date), then finding loads in one go, and finally the invoicing chain. If, for example, 60 % of calls come between 7:00 and 9:00 and between 14:00 and 16:00, move routine tasks out of those hours and ask for the sign-off as soon as the load has arrived, not by phone the next morning.

RAHTIS on the same principle

In RAHTIS, the customer can see the stages of the job and the estimated time of arrival via the tracking link, so there are fewer "where's the lorry?" calls. The driver signs off the delivery in the app, an invoice to your own customer is created from the job and payment status is tracked in the same place: https://www.rahtis.eu/en.

In a small firm where you handle dispatch, invoicing and safety yourself, smoothing out workload peaks means the same as with electricity: less overlapping load in the busiest hours, and a measurable result. Do the heaviest work when the grid or your calendar has slack, not when everyone else is trying to do the same.

FAQ

How much is the demand charge in Finland, and where can I see it?

The price and the basis of calculation vary between network operators, so there is no general figure. Check your network contract or your network operator's price list to see whether your tariff has a demand charge, its unit price in euros per kilowatt per month and how the billed power is determined. For example, in the 2026 price lists the demand charge for low-voltage demand tariffs was about €1.3/kW/month at Kuopion Sähköverkko and about €3/kW/month for Elenia's large-customer demand tariff.

Can I identify the peaks myself, or do I need a separate meter?

You can identify them yourself. The metering data are in Datahub, and you can download them as a CSV file from the Datahub customer portal or your network operator's online service. A separate meter is not essential, but your own sub-meter gives a more precise picture of the load from individual appliances.

How long a period is needed to identify the peaks?

12 months is a suitable period. It covers both the winter heating peaks and the summer, so you see the variation over the whole year. A shorter period can be misleading if, for example, the peak only occurs on freezing mornings.

Will the connection charge go down if consumption is staggered?

Not directly. Staggering reduces the demand charge, if you have one, but the connection charge is determined by the size of the connection. Downsizing the connection and its effect on charges are agreed with the network operator under its connection terms.

Is it worth moving electric vehicle charging to the night if there are several charging points?

Yes, especially with several charging points. Several vehicles charging at once in the evening drive up power quickly, and depending on how the demand charge is calculated, a single peak hour can affect the bill for the whole month or even the whole year. Schedule charging for the night and stagger it so that the first vehicle starts charging at 22:00, the second at 23:00 and the third at midnight. Many chargers already support scheduling.

miten-etsia-luotettava-alihankkija-satul.title: How to find a reliable subcontractor for trailer and container swaps
miten-etsia-luotettava-alihankkija-satul.description: A reliable subcontractor for trailer and container swaps: checking licences and contractor's liability documents, liability questions and a scoring form.
miten-etsia-luotettava-alihankkija-satul.html:
Key takeaways

  • Before the first load, check the subcontractor's registration details, operator licence and carrier's liability insurance, plus the reports required under the Finnish Contractor's Liability Act where applicable.
  • Every trailer or container swap is a point where liability passes over, and it should be documented with a timestamp, unit numbers, the seal number and photos.
  • Agree the division of liability in writing before signing, even when the subcontractor was found on a freight exchange.
  • Score a new subcontractor on seven questions on a scale of 0–2: under 8 points means you look for someone else.
  • Reassess the subcontractor at 3, 6 and 12 months using the same criteria as at the start.

For trailer and container swaps, you find a reliable subcontractor with three checks: that the business and its licences are legitimate, proven experience of exactly this kind of trailer and container work, and a written division of liability before the first load. This guide gives you a step-by-step assessment process, the liability questions and a printable form, which also work for agreements made via a freight exchange.

How do you find a reliable subcontractor for swaps without unnecessary risk?

The subcontractor runs part of the transport, but towards your customer you are usually the one who is responsible for it: if the subcontractor operates without a valid operator licence or insurance, you may end up bearing the delay, the damage or the consequences yourself. The EU regulation on the occupation of road transport operator requires operators to have, among other things, good repute, appropriate financial standing and professional competence (Regulation (EC) No 1071/2009, EUR-Lex). This guide moves from checking legitimacy to assessing operational capability, liability questions and a ready-made form.

A small haulage firm has no separate vetting team, so the process has to be quick and repeatable. Every new subcontractor goes through the same sequence: paperwork, equipment, references and contract. Once the process is established, assessing one subcontractor takes about half an hour. That is a small effort compared with being left without compensation when a €30,000 load is damaged during a swap.

What do trailer and container swaps mean in terms of liability?

In a swap, a semi-trailer or container changes tractor unit or driver partway through the transport chain. Every swap is a point where liability passes over: the condition of the load, the trailer and the seals is checked, and that check decides who is liable for any damage. If a swap is done without a documented inspection, the evidence is weakest for whoever has the poorest paperwork.

Liability points in a trailer swap

The chain is usually collection, swap, onward transport and handover. For each point there should be a timestamped confirmation showing the registration numbers, the seal number, the number of packages and any discrepancies. Without them, you cannot show that the damage occurred during the subcontractor's leg and not yours. In the RAHTIS driver app, the driver photographs every side of the trailer, the seal and any new damage, and at delivery the photo taken at collection is shown alongside for comparison (RAHTIS and trailer swaps).

The choice of swap location affects the risk: a lit terminal area with CCTV is safer than a dark lay-by. If the subcontractor suggests a swap location without surveillance or lighting, ask why. Agree the swap location in advance and make sure both drivers have access to it.

Special issues in container haulage

With a container, the seal and the container's condition are key evidence: an intact seal, recorded on the consignment note at the time of handover, supports the case that the contents were not tampered with during transport, but on its own it does not decide liability. Ask the subcontractor in advance how they record the seal number and the container inspection. Note that Incoterms, such as FCA or EXW, divide costs and risk between seller and buyer. Liability between you and your subcontractor is decided by the contract of carriage and the applicable law: the CMR Convention for international carriage, and the Finnish Road Transport Contracts Act for domestic carriage.

In container haulage, handling at the port and terminal can cause delays that do not show up in the driver's paperwork. Ask the subcontractor who pays for waiting at the terminal and what happens if a container waits 12 hours for a crane. If the subcontractor cannot answer, they have probably not hauled containers before.

How do you know the subcontractor exists and operates legally?

Before you pass a load on, check a few things. They take a quarter of an hour but prevent the typical pitfalls: the business does not exist, the operator licence is missing or the insurance does not cover the carrier's liability.

Mandatory documents

Ask for copies of the following and file them so they can be found later:

  • Trade register extract: for a Finnish company, the details are available free of charge from YTJ (the Finnish Business Information System); for a foreign company, from the company register in its home country. Check that the company is not bankrupt and that its line of business is transport.
  • VAT number: the VAT identification number of a company from another EU country is checked in the EU's VIES service.
  • Operator licence: in Finland, professional goods transport with a vehicle over 3.5 tonnes requires a goods transport licence issued by Traficom, and international transport requires an EU Community licence. Since 21 May 2022, international transport with vehicles of 2.5–3.5 tonnes has also required a licence. Ask for a copy; do not settle for verbal assurances.
  • Carrier's liability insurance (CMR insurance): general business liability insurance alone does not cover the carrier's liability for the goods carried. Check the maximum cover and validity of the policy.
  • Reports under the Contractor's Liability Act: if the value of the subcontract is at least €9,000 excluding VAT and the work relates to your normal operations, such as regular transports, the Finnish Act on the Contractor's Obligations and Liability when Work is Contracted Out requires you to obtain, before signing, among other things a trade register extract, proof of registration in the prepayment register, the employer register and the VAT register, a tax debt certificate or a statement on tax debt, a pension insurance certificate, and information on the applicable collective agreement and occupational health care (Contractor's Liability Act 1233/2006, Finlex).

If the subcontractor drags their feet over the documents, that is an answer too. A serious subcontractor usually sends the paperwork the same day. If it takes three days to get a copy of the operator licence, consider how quickly they will respond when the load is on the road and something goes wrong.

Credit information

In Finland, payment default records and company financial information are available from credit reference services such as Asiakastieto or Dun & Bradstreet. For a foreign company, equivalent information is available from credit reference services in its own country. Also check whether the company was set up only a few months ago: a new company is not automatically bad, but it warrants a smaller first load and closer monitoring.

A single payment default record is not automatic grounds for rejection, but it changes the terms. Do not make advance payments to a company with outstanding payment defaults. One record may be due to a temporary cash-flow problem, but several records point to a systematic problem.

How do you assess a subcontractor's operational capability in practice?

Operational capability shows in three things: the condition of the equipment, the drivers' language skills and how quickly the subcontractor responds during the day. In trailer swaps, the schedule is everything, so ask directly how quickly you will get a status update on the load. If the answer is "I'll call when I can", keep looking.

Equipment questions

Ask for the registration numbers and to see the latest periodic roadworthiness inspection (katsastus) and a summary of the service history. Check that the tractor unit has a fifth wheel suitable for trailer swaps and the necessary connections. For a one-lorry operator, a single breakdown can stop the whole chain, so ask what happens if the vehicle is stuck in the workshop midweek.

Also ask the age of the equipment. A trailer over 15 years old is not automatically bad, but the brakes and air suspension need closer inspection. If the subcontractor has only one vehicle, make sure they have a contingency plan: their own spare equipment or an agreement with another operator.

Reference questions

Ask for the contact details of two previous clients and call them yourself. Ask three things: did the vehicle leave on schedule, did the proof of delivery come back in order, and was more invoiced than agreed? Record the answers in the same place as the subcontractor's other details.

A reference call is not a formality. Ask concrete questions: was the load on time, what was done when something went wrong, and would the referee use the subcontractor again? If the answer is a hesitant "I suppose so", treat it as a no. If the referee describes precisely how the subcontractor dealt with a delay or damage, that tells you it is a professional operator.

What questions on the division of liability must you ask before the contract?

Liability questions

Ask these before you put a single run in the calendar. Who pays if the load is damaged in a trailer swapped by the subcontractor, or the trailer comes back damaged? Who bears the risk if container handling at the port or terminal causes a delay or damage? How are delays dealt with: who informs the end customer, who pays the extra costs and on what timescale?

Who handles the consignment note and the proof of delivery, and can your customer see them directly? Who is responsible for ADR requirements if the load is dangerous goods? And who bears the risk of an empty return if the subcontractor is left without a backload?

Go through the list in writing, because a verbal "yes, we'll sort it" is no help once the damage has happened. Freight exchanges such as TIMOCOM and Trans.eu describe their own terms of use and member checks on their websites, but they do not replace the contract between you and your subcontractor. In RAHTIS, the job details, photos, consignment note and proof of delivery build up on the same transport, but the division of liability is still agreed in the contract between you.

Contract terms

Write down the terms: liability for damage, the consequences of delay (or the absence of any), payment terms and cancellation terms. A verbal agreement is quick to make, but a written one settles a dispute. Also define what happens if the subcontractor cancels midweek: do they cover the extra cost of a replacement transport, or does each side bear its own losses?

How do you use the assessment form in practice?

Form template

Print the form and fill it in for every new subcontractor before the first load. The form has three sections: legitimacy, operational capability and division of liability. If any point is left blank, do not send a load until the answer is on paper.

#QuestionSection
1Business ID (Y-tunnus) or foreign registration number, VAT number and register extract checked?Legitimacy
2Operator licence and carrier's liability insurance valid?Legitimacy
3Equipment, roadworthiness inspection and service history checked?Operational capability
4Drivers experienced in similar swaps and loads?Operational capability
5Liability limit and division of damage agreed in writing?Liability
6Agreed who pays for waiting, terminal charges and inspections?Liability
7Practice for consignment notes, photos and proof of delivery agreed?Liability

Scoring

Give each point 0 (no answer), 1 (incomplete) or 2 (in order). A total of 12–14 points means you can send the load. 8–11 points means the gaps are put right in writing first. Under 8 points means you look for another subcontractor.

Do the scoring even when the subcontractor was found on a freight exchange: Trans.eu, TIMOCOM and Teleroute show basic details, but they do not answer these questions for you. When you have to choose between two subcontractors, the scores make the choice justifiable. Without scoring, the choice rests on gut feeling, and gut feeling is a poor justification when the damage exceeds the insurance.

How do subcontracting arrangements made via a freight exchange differ from your own customers?

Platform checks

TIMOCOM, Teleroute and Trans.eu each check their members' company details in their own way, but no platform does the assessment for you. A platform check is a baseline, not a guarantee. Check the company's registration and credit details yourself before the load: in Finland, registration details are available free of charge from YTJ, and payment default information from credit reference services.

The platforms' own ratings and reviews are useful, but the criteria behind them are not always public, and they do not tell you whether the subcontractor's insurance is valid right now. Use the platform's rating as a filter, not as the decision.

What the platform does not cover

Subcontracting via a freight exchange differs from an established working relationship: the division of liability, liability for damage and the special requirements of swaps have to be agreed by you, because the exchange's general terms know nothing about the risk points of a trailer swap. Use the same form as for other subcontractors, and agree the consignment note and proof of delivery practice before the first run. The platform tells you the company exists; you assess whether it handles swaps properly.

How does RAHTIS help with subcontractor management, and where does it fall short?

What RAHTIS takes care of

On the RAHTIS load board, you can see each haulier's vehicle details, ratings, punctuality history and a Verified badge. The badge means that RAHTIS staff have checked the documents the company has submitted under the Contractor's Liability Act, such as the trade register extract, tax and pension insurance certificates and insurance, and recorded the date until which the check is valid. During the transport, photos, seals, the consignment note and the proof of delivery build up on the same job, so documenting swaps does not rely on memory.

What you have to do yourself

The Verified badge tells you the documents are in order, but not whether the subcontractor is right for your particular swaps and containers. Equipment, references, the division of liability and the assessment form remain your job, as covered above. The system shows what has been agreed and what has happened, but you build the trust yourself.

How do you build a long-term subcontractor relationship?

After the first load, the subcontractor has passed the check, but reliability is built through repeated success. That is why the first year is decisive. Reassess the subcontractor at 3, 6 and 12 months using the same criteria as at the start: paperwork, equipment, division of liability and the number of delays.

Keep the assessment form a living document. When the subcontractor runs a load, update the scores. When they are late or the proof of delivery is slow to arrive, record it. After three months you will see the trend: is performance improving or deteriorating? If the trend is bad, do not wait for damage; reduce their loads and move them to a subcontractor who performs better.

A long-term relationship does not mean automatic renewal. It means both sides know what to expect, and the contract is updated when circumstances change. If the insurance is renewed on different terms, ask for a new certificate. If the contract runs for more than 12 months, the Contractor's Liability Act requires the subcontractor to provide tax and pension insurance certificates again every 12 months. If the subcontractor acquires new equipment, check it before the first run.

FAQ

How much should the subcontractor's insurance cover?

Carrier's liability insurance must cover at least the statutory liability: in international carriage, 8.33 special drawing rights (SDR) per kilogram of gross weight of the goods under the CMR Convention, and in domestic carriage €20 per kilogram under the Finnish Road Transport Contracts Act. Ask for the insurance certificate and check its validity. If the value of the load exceeds the liability limit, the consignor can declare a higher value for the goods in the consignment note against an agreed surcharge, or take out separate cargo insurance for the goods. Agree this in writing before the first run.

Can I use a subcontractor found on a freight exchange without doing my own background check?

It is not a good idea. TIMOCOM, Trans.eu and Teleroute check their members' basic details in different ways, but that is a baseline, not a guarantee. Check the registration details, operator licence and insurance certificate yourself, plus the reports under the Contractor's Liability Act where required, and fill in the same assessment form as for other subcontractors.

What do I do if the subcontractor damages a trailer during a swap?

If you have a timestamped confirmation of the swap with photos, unit numbers and the seal number, you can show that the damage occurred during the subcontractor's leg. Without a documented inspection, it is one word against another. That is why the division of liability is agreed in writing in advance, not after the damage.

Do I need a written contract for one-off subcontracting?

Yes. Being a one-off does not remove the liability points: liability for damage, handling of delays, payment terms and cancellation terms should be recorded even for a single run. An email in which the terms have been accepted is often enough. Also agree the consignment note and proof of delivery practice before the run, so the evidence exists if something goes wrong.

How do I check the background of a foreign subcontractor?

Start with the trade register in the company's home country, the equivalent of Finland's YTJ. Check the VAT number in the EU's VIES service if it is an EU company. Ask for a copy of the Community licence for international transport, and look up payment default information from a credit reference service in that country. A new company is not automatically bad, but it warrants a smaller first load and closer monitoring.

miten-laatia-rahtitarjous-nopeasti-asiak.title: How to put together a haulage quote for a customer quickly
miten-laatia-rahtitarjous-nopeasti-asiak.description: Build a haulage quote in minutes from seven fields: route, load, vehicle, price, validity, payment terms and contact details. Send it while still on the call.
miten-laatia-rahtitarjous-nopeasti-asiak.html:
Key takeaways

  • Build your haulage quote from seven fields: company details, route, load details, vehicle type, price with justification, validity period and payment terms.
  • Unless a return load is confirmed, price in empty running using the kilometres for both directions, and tell the customer so plainly.
  • Always state the validity period, for example seven days; otherwise the quote stays open forever and the price of fuel may change.
  • Justify the price with the route, vehicle type and schedule rather than discounts, and most price haggling stops of its own accord.
  • A freight exchange gives you ready-made load details and a guide to the going rate, to which you add your own margin; RAHTIS keeps the job, the CMR and the invoice in one workflow.

Put together a haulage quote in minutes by filling in seven fields: company details, route, vehicle type, price and its justification, validity period, payment terms and contact details. With the structure ready as a template, the quote goes to the customer while you are still on the phone, not a day later after being scribbled in a notebook. This guide shows how to do it in practice, field by field. If you want a broader overview of transport management and the freight exchange, take a look at RAHTIS – Transport management and freight exchange: loose trailers, containers and express deliveries.

How do you put together a haulage quote for a customer quickly?

In five minutes, if the information is to hand and you know the structure by heart: origin and destination, type of load, weight and volume, schedule, price and payment terms. Write these seven lines in the same order every time and the quote takes shape during the call rather than afterwards in a notebook.

Base the price on your own costs per kilometre and per hour. You can follow how those costs change in the road haulage cost index published by Statistics Finland, which the industry association SKAL (Finnish Transport and Logistics) helped to develop. Once the basis is clear, the quote can be justified straight away. In RAHTIS (rahtis.eu/fi) you can see the profitability of each vehicle: job revenue minus fuel, driver pay and other costs.

Speed comes from repetition. If you always use the same template, nobody needs to do creative writing in the middle of a busy call. Start the call by asking about the route and the load, after which the price is the only open variable. Enter the answers straight into the ready-made fields and send the message as soon as the call ends.

What information must a haulage quote contain?

Company details and the customer

Start the quote with your company details: name, Business ID, address and a contact person with phone number. Do the same for the customer, so that the documents later match the consignment note and the invoice. Without a Business ID the customer cannot check who they are handing their load to.

A missing Business ID causes invoicing delays and possible mix-ups if there are several companies with the same name. Make sure the contact person is the one who actually makes the decisions, not someone who just passes messages on. This shortens the approval process considerably.

Route, vehicle type and load details

This is the heart of the quote. Write down the details that determine the price and prevent misunderstandings about the load:

FieldExampleWhy it matters
Origin and destinationVantaa → TampereDistance determines the price and the empty running
Load8 Euro pallets, 6,000 kgDetermines the vehicle type
Vehicle typeSemi-trailer, drawbar trailer, tankerWrong type = cancellation
ScheduleCollection Thursday 8–12, delivery FridayUrgency costs extra
Additional servicesUnloading, loading, temperature monitoringA hidden cost if forgotten

If the load needs a specialist vehicle or ADR certification, say so plainly in the quote. Fewer questions later.

Giving the load dimensions in metres and kilograms is more precise than a pallet count alone. For example, "8 pallets, 120×80×200 cm, 6,000 kg in total" gives the driver confidence that the load will fit and stay within the weight limits. If you leave out the dimensions, the customer may assume standard-size pallets when the load is in fact out of gauge.

Validity period and payment terms

Without a validity period the quote stays open forever, and the price of fuel may change before the customer replies. State, for example, "valid for 7 days", or tie the price to a specific departure date. Payment terms belong in the quote from the start: 14 days net is common, and if the customer insists on 30 days, agree it before the job, not when you send the invoice. The RAHTIS API documentation (https://www.rahtis.eu/fi/api-docs) shows how a shipper's system passes the order details to RAHTIS without retyping.

The validity period protects you against swings in market prices, especially fuel. If you tie the price to a specific departure date, the customer understands that delays may lead to a new quote. Stating the payment terms in the quote prevents surprises at invoicing and gives the customer a chance to comment on the terms before the job starts.

How do you price a haulage job in minutes?

Fixed price or hourly rate

Choose the model according to the nature of the job. A fixed price suits regular runs where the route and the type of work are known in advance. An hourly rate makes sense when the work includes unloading, waiting or several drops that you cannot estimate beforehand.

The advantage of a fixed price is predictability for the customer: they know the exact sum in advance and need not fear unexpected costs. The advantage of an hourly rate is on your side: if unloading drags on or the customer is late, you invoice for the work done. Many hauliers use a hybrid: a fixed price for the basic job and an hourly rate for extra work, such as waiting beyond the agreed time.

Empty running and return loads

Let us work through an example you can apply directly to your own jobs. Start from a rate per kilometre that covers fuel, the driver's wages, insurance and vehicle wear, and add your margin. If the customer's job is 300 km but there is no confirmed return load for the journey home, price it on 600 kilometres, i.e. both directions. This is fair, because an empty kilometre costs you almost as much as a loaded one.

Tell the customer plainly that the price includes the empty leg; that way the justification is ready and neither side has to guess. If you get a return load from the freight exchange or from your own customers, you can take the empty running out and offer a more competitive price. In RAHTIS you see board jobs near your drop-off and can offer the spare capacity of a lorry already on the road (sign up: https://www.rahtis.eu/et/apply), so a return load can cover part of the journey before the quote goes out.

A concrete example: the rate is €1.20 per kilometre and the margin is 15 per cent. A one-way 300 km job with no return load costs 600 km × €1.20 × 1.15 = €828. If you find a return load, the price drops to 300 km × €1.20 × 1.15 = €414. That €414 difference is your room to negotiate while still keeping your margin.

Which extra costs to include

Include a waiting time agreement (e.g. first hour free, hourly rate after that), ferry and road tolls, a fuel surcharge and handling of the CMR consignment note. Traficom (the Finnish Transport and Communications Agency) provides guidance on consignment note and CMR requirements in road transport (Traficom), so make sure your extra charges also cover the documentation, whether electronic or on paper.

Forgetting extra costs is the most common reason a profitable job turns into a loss-maker. For example, occasional waiting at the delivery point can stretch to hours, and if you have not agreed compensation, you are doing it in your own time. Always state the waiting terms in the quote: the first hour is included in the price, after that €45–60 per hour.

How do you justify the price to the customer without haggling?

A good quote justifies the price with the route, vehicle type and schedule, not with discounts. When the quote shows the kilometres, the nature of the route (for example a one-way run with no return load), the type of vehicle needed and the collection and delivery times, the customer can see where the money goes. Empty running and the lack of a return route are real costs, and showing them openly stops most price haggling.

Also state what is included: the consignment note (CMR), waiting time terms and payment terms. When everything is in writing, the negotiation moves from details to the overall price, which you have already justified.

The same principle works for your own customers and for jobs from the freight exchange. Once a quote has been built properly, the next one goes out as a copy. Keep a reusable quote template for your own routes; you can join RAHTIS at https://www.rahtis.eu/fi/apply, from a single lorry upwards.

Justification matters even more when you are competing with larger operators. Big companies can offer a low rate per kilometre, but they carry overheads and delays. Your advantage is speed and flexibility. When you base the price realistically on costs and show the calculation openly, a small haulier can win a tender against a bigger operator, because the customer understands how the price is made up and trusts it.

How do you send the quote and follow up the reply?

Email works for regular customers, but the message easily gets lost in the customer's inbox. Freight exchange messaging is the fastest way to reach those looking for transport: Teleroute, TIMOCOM and Trans.eu, for example, handle the quote and the reply in the same system, so you have a written record of the price and terms (how a freight exchange works).

Choose the channel to suit the job: email for a regular customer, the freight exchange for an empty leg, RAHTIS when you want everything in one place. In RAHTIS the shipper publishes the job once, carriers reply directly with offers and the transport progresses step by step in the same view: https://www.rahtis.eu/lt/apply.

Follow-up is the part that a notebook-and-spreadsheet setup loses. Set a reminder for 24 hours later: if there is no reply, call or send a follow-up message. Log every quote you send and its status (pending, rejected, accepted), so you can see each week which customers and which routes actually pay.

Following up quotes is a numbers game. If you send ten quotes a week and three are left hanging without a reply, you are losing potential turnover. A simple spreadsheet with columns for customer, route, price, date sent and status is enough to get started. When you see, for example, that 80 per cent of your quotes on the Helsinki–Turku route are accepted, you can focus more on it.

How does a freight exchange speed up the quoting process?

What freight exchanges offer for quoting

A freight exchange gives you ready-made load details that you would otherwise collect by phone and write in a notebook: origin and destination, date, trailer type, weight and load description. When a customer asks for a quote, you check the price level for a comparable route on the exchange and add your own margin on top. TIMOCOM and Trans.eu, for example, provide route-level price data or a price forecast, and you decide whether to go below or above it.

The exchange also shortens negotiation. When the customer sees that there is demand on the route, your price is easier to accept without a long tussle.

Seeing the market rate gives you a realistic idea of the prices other operators are working at. If your own price is clearly above the market, you can either lower it or justify the difference: faster delivery, fewer delays or better customer service. If your price is below the market, you can raise your margin without losing the customer.

RAHTIS on routes and empty legs

In RAHTIS the whole chain is in one place: the shipper publishes a load or a trailer swap once, you see empty legs and return loads on your own route, and quote directly on the basis of the same information. Once the job is accepted, it carries on as a transport, a consignment note and an invoice without you moving data between the exchange, a spreadsheet and a notebook.

An honest limitation: RAHTIS is not yet as large an international marketplace as the established exchanges, so for finding loads abroad you may need another exchange alongside it.

How does RAHTIS handle the quote and the transport in one place?

RAHTIS brings together the same steps that a haulier with four lorries described on Reddit: separate freight exchange logins, an outdated TMS and a paper notebook of who owes what (Reddit thread on a small haulier's working day). In RAHTIS the quote is made once, the customer accepts it and the same job carries on through the workflow without copy-pasting.

While the job is under way, the driver and the shipper follow its status step by step, the driver scans the consignment note (CMR) into the system with the app and, after the POD, the invoice is recorded on the same job, where its due date is tracked. You do not need to move data separately from a quote spreadsheet to invoicing software and a notebook.

To be honest, RAHTIS does not replace everything: its offer desk is not a marketplace open to everyone like Trans.eu or Teleroute; a job goes to approved, suitable vehicles in the area, and it does not have the range of enterprise add-ons that McLeod or Turvo offer. RAHTIS is designed for small hauliers, from a single lorry upwards, and its strength is precisely that the quote, the transport and the invoice live in the same workflow instead of in three different programs.

Joining up the workflow saves time, but even more important is the reduction in errors. When you move data by hand from the quote to the consignment note and from there to the invoice, every transfer is a chance to type the wrong address, weight or price. In a single system the data stays unchanged from start to finish, and the customer receives the correct invoice at the correct address.

What are the most common mistakes in a haulage quote and how do you avoid them?

The first mistake is a missing validity period. Without a date the quote lives forever, and the customer may come back three weeks later demanding the same price even though fuel prices have changed. Always add a line saying "quote valid for 7 days" or similar.

The second mistake is a vague vehicle type. "Lorry" does not tell anyone whether the job suits a semi-trailer, a swap body or a van. If the customer assumes something else and you send the wrong vehicle, the empty running is at your expense. State the type, volume and payload.

The third mistake is forgetting the payment terms. An agreement noted in a paper notebook without terms means that who owes what is left to your memory. State the payment period, for example 14 days net, and whether you charge interest on late payment.

These three lines take a minute but save negotiation and debt-chasing later.

The fourth mistake is missing detail in the load description. "Pallets" is not enough, as pallets can come in different sizes and contain different goods. State the number of pallets, the dimensions and the weight, so the driver knows what they are collecting and what space the load will fit in. The fifth mistake is forgetting additional services: if the customer expects unloading and you have priced only the transport, the job becomes a loss-maker.

FAQ

Can I send a haulage quote directly to a freight exchange without a customer of my own?

Yes, you can. Freight exchanges such as Teleroute, TIMOCOM and Trans.eu list open loads that you can respond to directly in the system without an existing customer relationship. The exchange gives you the details ready-made: route, date, vehicle type, weight and load description. You add your own margin and submit the quote. This works particularly well for filling empty legs.

What should I do if the customer asks for a discount on the quote?

If the quote justifies the price with the route, vehicle type, kilometres and schedule, most price haggling stops of its own accord. When the customer sees where the money goes, the negotiation moves to the overall price. If a discount is still requested, see whether a return load is available: it lets you take out the empty running, making the price genuinely more competitive without the deal becoming a loss.

How long is a haulage quote valid by default?

There should be no default: always state the validity period, for example seven days. Without a date the quote remains open forever, and the customer may come back weeks later demanding the same price even though fuel has gone up. Alternatively, you can tie the price to a specific departure date, so the schedule sets the validity for you.

Do I need a separate TMS if I only send a few quotes a week?

Not necessarily. A notebook and a spreadsheet work until the quote, the consignment note and the invoice live in different places and the data has to be moved by hand. For a small haulier, from a single lorry upwards, RAHTIS handles the quote, the transport, the CMR and the invoice in one workflow without copy-pasting. Once the quote template has been built, the next quote goes out as a copy in minutes.

miten-loittaa-palautuskuorma-tyhjelle-au.title: How to find a return load for an empty lorry
miten-loittaa-palautuskuorma-tyhjelle-au.description: How to find a return load for an empty lorry: channels in order of priority, a margin decision tree and a routine that replaces hit-and-miss load hunting.
miten-loittaa-palautuskuorma-tyhjelle-au.html:
Key takeaways

  • Look for a return load in a fixed order: your own customers first, then freight exchanges along the route, and terminals and ports last.
  • Compare every load with the cost of running empty: the freight rate minus fuel, tolls and extra working hours decides whether the load is worth taking.
  • Before quoting, check four points: route, timing, equipment and payment terms; if one fails, running home empty is often the cheaper option.
  • Write your offer precisely: equipment, available time, route, price and driver details, so the shipper replies to you.
  • Check the payment period and the payment default register before committing; late payment interest is governed by the Finnish Interest Act and compensation for collection costs by the Debt Collection Act.

Check your channels in a fixed order: your own customers first, then freight exchanges along your route, then other hauliers in the same area. Assess each load with a decision tree: route, timing, equipment and payment terms. This article gives you both in concrete terms, plus a routine that replaces hit-and-miss hunting.

What is a return load and why is an empty lorry a cost risk?

A return load, or backhaul, is freight you take on for the journey home when your own customer's job or a freight exchange job ends in the wrong place. Empty running means the same journey with no load and no income. Freight exchanges such as Trans.eu and Teleroute list these return loads all the time, and RAHTIS shows on its own offer desk the jobs near the place where each of your vehicles frees up, with those heading towards home first (https://www.rahtis.eu/fi).

Empty running is not just fuel: it is lost margin

An empty lorry has the same cost structure as a loaded one: fuel, the driver's wages, insurance, tyres and depreciation all run, but no money comes in. In European road haulage roughly a fifth of vehicle-kilometres are driven empty, which is capacity wasted outright (Eurostat, Road freight transport statistics).

When you run 300 kilometres empty, you do not just lose fuel. You lose the amount the return load would have brought in, less fuel and tolls. That is why looking for return loads should be a routine, not hit-and-miss hunting.

Which channels should you search for return loads first, and in what order?

It pays to dig for return loads in a set order: your own customers first, then regular partners, then freight exchanges and terminals last. The order is based on where you get the best price and the least risk relative to the time spent searching.

1. Your own customers and regular partners

Call or message the customers and subcontracting partners whose routes cross the route of your empty lorry. You already know how they pay and what equipment they need, so the negotiation takes a minute. Ask in particular about regular loads on set weekdays: one fixed return load a week is worth more than a one-off load.

2. Freight exchanges and load boards

If your own network turns up nothing, open the freight exchanges. Those used in Finland and Northern Europe include Teleroute, TIMOCOM and Trans.eu; an option that combines transport management with its own offer desk is RAHTIS (https://www.rahtis.eu/sv). The biggest difference between the channels is how quickly you see new loads along your route.

ChannelSearch based onMain benefitsDrawbacks
Own customersPhone and emailPrice, reliable payment termsLimited volume, relies on memory
Freight exchangeRoute and equipment searchLarge number of loads, speedPrice competition, unknown counterparty
TerminalOn site or by phoneLoose trailer and port loads close byUncertain schedules, tight pricing

3. Terminals, ports and loose trailer traffic

Last of all, check the terminals and ports along the route: loose trailer and container loads often only appear on the day. These carry the highest risk, because waiting times and payment terms vary, so take them only when the other channels have come up empty.

How do route and timing affect which loads are worth offering to carry?

The direction of the route, when loads are posted and how flexible the load is decide which return loads are realistically available. The same lorry gets different results on a different day and on a different corridor.

Route direction and the rhythm of port traffic

Empty running is most likely in the direction where the least freight moves. Loose trailers leaving ports and industrial hubs head inland on weekday mornings, so an empty lorry at a port in the afternoon is competing for very few loads. The opposite direction, from rural areas to the hubs, often offers more jobs but lower rates. Equipment narrows the choice: a reefer load will not be offered to a flatbed, and a required loading time rules out long repositioning runs.

Timing: when loads are posted and when they disappear

Freight exchanges such as Teleroute and TIMOCOM post loads around the clock, but in practice new offers tend to appear in the mornings and afternoons, and urgent ones are gone within hours. If your lorry will be empty at 12 noon tomorrow, offer to take loads whose collection time is flexible, and keep your phone free for the morning posting window. Jobs published in RAHTIS are visible step by step, so you can follow the shipper's schedule changes without calling; the terms of use state that the shipper may cancel an assignment before it is completed and that the haulier is notified of the cancellation (https://www.rahtis.eu/fi/kayttoehdot). Speed of response often matters more than price.

How do you decide whether to take a return load or run home empty?

An empty journey home always costs money: fuel, time and wear accumulate even though there is no income. A return load is almost always worth taking if it covers the variable costs and leaves even a small margin. The sum is simple: the freight rate offered minus fuel, tolls and extra working hours. If what is left is more than the cost of running empty, the load wins.

Decision tree: four questions before you quote

Before quoting, go through four points in this order. The first is the route: does the load take you towards your next job or your home base, or do you have to go 200 km out of your way, making the actual journey longer? The second is timing: can loading and unloading be done before the job you have already agreed, and is there enough buffer for delays? The third is equipment: do the trailer type, lifting gear or heating meet the load's requirements, or would you need extra kit you do not otherwise carry? The fourth is payment terms: ask about the payment period straight away, and if it is 60 days or more, price the delay in or do not quote. If any of the four fails, running home empty is often cheaper than taking a bad load.

Checklist: equipment, weight, time, payment terms

Before quoting, check: the total weight and floor area of the load against your own equipment, the loading and unloading times (unpaid waiting hours can eat the margin), tolls and ferry fares on the route, and the consignment note details (the CMR in international transport) in advance. Also bear in mind the risk that there will be no next load ready at the delivery point.

All in all, the decision is the same every time: work out the margin, compare it with the cost of running empty and decide within five minutes. RAHTIS shows the route and timing of a job and the shipper's payment history in the same view, so comparing is quicker than leafing through a notebook and separate exchange logins (https://www.rahtis.eu/et). The system does not make the decision for you, but it removes the searching, which is often the reason bad loads are taken in a rush.

What should you put in a load offer to get a reply?

An offer that gets a reply contains five points: equipment (e.g. crane or refrigerated equipment, payload), availability window in hours, route from collection to delivery and return, price and driver details. Write the price clearly: is it fixed or negotiable, and does it include waiting time?

Add one line that makes the biggest difference: "Available [date, time] on [town]–[town], equipment [specify], price [€]." A vague "we have space" is ignored, because the shipper is comparing dozens of offers within minutes.

Driver details and liability issues are best agreed in writing at the offer stage, since in international transport the entries in the consignment note are evidence of the terms of the contract of carriage, and the carrier's liability is determined by the CMR Convention (Articles 17–29 of the CMR Convention). In RAHTIS the offer and the job details travel in the same system, so they do not have to be copied onto paper; the features are listed in more detail in the product description.

How do you avoid the payment and liability risks of return loads?

A return load from a freight exchange often comes from an unknown shipper, so check their ability to pay before you commit. Ask directly about the payment period and, if necessary, ask for payment in advance on the first job. In Finland, late payment interest is governed by the Interest Act (korkolaki) (Finlex, Interest Act), and in business-to-business transactions the creditor is also entitled to a fixed €40 compensation for collection costs under the Debt Collection Act (perintälaki), so collecting overdue freight charges is not merely a matter for negotiation. Keep a record of each customer's payment times so you notice who repeatedly pays late.

Payment terms and credit information

The Finnish Trade Register shows that a company exists, but payment default information should be checked separately in a payment default register before a larger job. A security deposit or the shipper's ratings on the exchange (e.g. Trans.eu or TIMOCOM) gives an indication of how the shipper pays, but it does not replace your own judgement. Running home empty is sometimes cheaper than freight paid 60 days late.

CMR and liability for the load

Fill in the CMR consignment note carefully: a checked number of packages and reservations about the apparent condition of the goods and their packaging protect you in the event of damage. Under the CMR Convention, the carrier's liability is limited to 8.33 SDR per kilogram of gross weight of the goods lost or damaged (Article 23), and the carrier is relieved of liability if, for example, the damage is caused by the sender's fault or defective packing (Article 17); any defects you notice should be recorded as reservations on the document itself. A paper notebook is not enough as evidence if a dispute arises only weeks later.

How do you turn finding return loads into a regular routine rather than hit-and-miss hunting?

Hit-and-miss hunting means you open the exchange only when the lorry is already empty and the phone is ringing. A routine means that fleet status, alerts and the order of work are ready before you need them. Three steps are enough.

Recording fleet status in advance

Every morning, write down which lorry is where, where it is heading back to, when it will be free and what equipment it has (trailer, crane, temperature requirement). This takes five minutes and is the foundation of the whole routine, because without it you do not know what return load you are actually looking for. A paper notebook will do, but it is worth having the same information on your phone as well.

Alerts and filters on the exchange

Do not browse the freight exchange by hand. Set filters for your usual routes: origin, destination direction, date and equipment requirement, and switch on alerts for new postings. When an offer comes in, reply quickly with a complete offer whose structure is already ready from previous jobs.

One tool instead of several exchanges

Several separate exchange and TMS logins are exactly the mess that eats up a one-person planner's day. In RAHTIS a job is recorded once and followed step by step, and consignment notes and payment tracking for invoices are handled in the same place. To be honest, RAHTIS does not bring external freight exchanges together in one view: it has its own offer desk where shippers publish jobs, so browsing other exchanges remains your responsibility. The routine stays the same though: record your fleet, let the alerts do the work for you and reply quickly.

FAQ

The return load does not cover the whole journey – is it still worth taking?
