Often, yes. Work out the margin for the whole journey: the freight rate offered minus fuel, tolls and extra working hours, and compare the result with the cost of the empty kilometres. If a part-journey load covers the variable costs and leaves even a small margin, it beats running empty. The exception is a detour that lengthens the overall journey too much.

How long before an empty run should you start looking for a return load?

As soon as you know when the lorry will be free and what the return route is, which is often a day or two before the empty run. Loads appear on the exchanges in the mornings and afternoons, and urgent ones are gone within hours. Set up filters and alerts in advance so that you see new loads straight away without constant browsing.

Can a return load be priced lower than normal freight, and how do I justify the price?

Yes, it can, because the lorry is heading back anyway. Justify the offer by the fact that the load fits a route and time already planned: collection and delivery fit the agreed times, the equipment is the right type and there is no extra mileage. State the price precisely and say whether waiting time is included, so that the shipper can compare easily.

What do I do if the shipper of a return load does not pay?

Ask about the payment period at the offer stage and keep a record of customers' payment times. In Finland, late payment interest on overdue freight charges is based on the Interest Act and compensation for collection costs on the Debt Collection Act, so collection is not merely a matter for negotiation. For larger jobs, check the payment default register in advance; if the payment period is 60 days or more, price the delay in or do not quote.

Do I need a separate contract or a CMR for a return load taken from an exchange?

The CMR Convention applies to international road carriage where the places of collection and delivery are in two different states, at least one of which is a contracting state; in that case a CMR consignment note is needed. Domestic carriage in Finland is governed by the Road Transport Contracts Act (tiekuljetussopimuslaki), under which a consignment note is made out unless the sender and the carrier agree otherwise. Fill in the consignment note carefully: a checked number of packages and reservations about the apparent condition of the goods protect you if there is damage. Driver details and liability issues are best agreed in writing at the offer stage, since the liability rules are binding. Each exchange's terms of use supplement the contract but do not replace the entries in the consignment note.

miten-seurata-kuormaa-vaihe-vaiheelta-as.title: How to give your customer step-by-step tracking of a load
miten-seurata-kuormaa-vaihe-vaiheelta-as.description: Step-by-step load tracking for your customer: a tracking link with no login, timestamped stages, an estimated time of arrival and proof of delivery.
miten-seurata-kuormaa-vaihe-vaiheelta-as.html:
Key takeaways

  • All the customer needs to know is what stage the transport is at: confirmed, loaded, in transit, arrived, and delivered and signed for.
  • In RAHTIS, the customer opens the tracking page from a link without needing their own login, and sees the timestamped stages and the estimated time of arrival.
  • After delivery, the same page shows the consignment note, the name of the person who signed for the goods and photos from the delivery point, so nobody has to dig receipts out of their email.
  • The tracking page does not show the vehicle's position on a map, the driver's phone number or the freight rate; GPS data are used only to estimate the time of arrival.
  • You see delays yourself as alerts, and the customer sees the updated arrival estimate via the link; a shipper with its own system can receive events through the API.

The customer wants to know two things: what stage the transport is at and when it will arrive. When the driver confirms the stages in the app, the RAHTIS tracking link shows them to the customer with timestamps, so the customer does not need to call to ask where the load is. This guide goes through the stages and how to share tracking with your customer.

How does the customer order a transport and get access to tracking?

A job is created in RAHTIS when you enter your own customer's order, or forward the customer's order message as an email, PDF or image, from which the system creates a draft. When you enter the customer's email address, the customer receives a message saying who is handling the transport, with a link to the tracking page. From then on, the customer can see from the link what stage the transport is at without calling you. The features are summarised on the RAHTIS website.

The order confirmation is the first stage of tracking

The confirmation fixes what is being carried, when it is collected and where it is delivered. It is always worth confirming in writing, and in RAHTIS every job has its own number that stays with it throughout the transport. The tracking page shows when the transport was confirmed.

What the customer needs to provide when ordering

At a minimum: the collection and delivery addresses, the requested time, details of the goods and a contact person at each end. If the transport involves a trailer swap or a container, it should be recorded in the order straight away so that the stages are set up correctly. It is a good idea to agree the consignment note details at the same time.

What stages does a transport go through?

From the customer's point of view, a transport has five stages: confirmed, loaded, in transit, arrived and delivered. Each stage tells the customer one thing: where things stand and when to expect the next change.

The stages in a table

StageWhat it meansWhat the customer sees on the tracking page
ConfirmedThe haulier has confirmed the job and assigned a vehicleThe haulier, the route and the planned times
LoadedThe driver has confirmed the loading point as completedArrival and departure times at the loading point
In transitThe vehicle is on its way to the next stopThe estimated time of arrival and what it is based on
ArrivedThe driver has arrived at the delivery pointThe arrival time
DeliveredUnloading has been signed forThe consignment note, the name of the person who signed and photos from the delivery point

When the stage changes and who changes it

The driver confirms the stages in the RAHTIS driver app: arrival and loading at the loading point, and arrival and unloading at the delivery point, where the driver takes the consignee's signature and photos. The tracking page updates according to these confirmations, without you having to pass on any information.

The tracking link can be forwarded, and anyone who receives it sees only this one transport. The tracking page is shown in the language selected in the link, and RAHTIS works in ten languages, including Swedish, Estonian, Latvian and Lithuanian.

Can the customer see the load's position in real time?

Not on a map. The RAHTIS tracking page shows an arrival estimate, not the vehicle's position. If a GPS fleet tracking system is connected to the vehicle (for example Wialon, Mapon, Webfleet or ABAX via an API key), the arrival estimate is calculated from the vehicle's latest position and the traffic situation. Otherwise the estimate is based on the route plan or the time given by the haulier, and the page states what the estimate is based on.

What the tracking page shows and what it does not

The page shows the haulier, the route, the stages with timestamps, the estimated time of arrival and, on Finnish roads, traffic announcements and road weather along the route. The vehicle's coordinates, the driver's phone number and the freight rate are not on the page. The position of a vehicle driven by an identifiable driver is personal data, so sharing it is restricted by the EU General Data Protection Regulation.

The driver's role

The driver does not need a separate device: they confirm the stages in the driver app, which also works offline and sends the confirmations once the connection returns. The app does not send a continuous position; the location data for the arrival estimate come from the vehicle's own tracking system, if one is connected.

How does information about delivery and delays get through?

Delivery and proof of delivery on the same page

Once unloading has been signed for, the consignment note, the name of the person who signed and photos from the delivery point appear on the tracking page. The driver takes them with the app, so you do not have to send PDFs as email attachments. The customer can see straight away what was delivered and when. The same job carries on into invoicing: when you create an invoice for your own customer, the sign-off and the consignment note are already on the job.

This does away with the situation where the customer calls asking for the signed delivery note, you search through a pile of paper and send a photo by WhatsApp an hour later.

Delays flagged before the customer has time to call

When a vehicle is running behind the planned time, you see it in RAHTIS as a delay alert, and the customer sees the updated arrival estimate on the tracking page. A shipper with its own system can also receive a webhook notification from RAHTIS, for example when the arrival estimate changes or the vehicle is more than 30 minutes late at a stop. When a delay is significant, it is still worth calling or writing to the customer yourself: a personal message about the new schedule is better service than just a changed time.

How do I track a transport involving a trailer swap or a container?

A multi-stage transport is not one journey but a chain: collection, a swap or terminal, and final delivery. When each point is on the job as its own waypoint, you can see at once where the chain has got to.

Tracking a trailer swap

When a semi-trailer changes tractor unit, the swap point is entered on the route as a stop in its own right. The customer sees in the tracking that the trailer is at the swap point and does not assume it has gone missing. When the swap point is confirmed, the tracking page updates without a separate phone call. More information on trailer swaps is on the page RAHTIS: trailer swap.

Container haulage from the port to the destination

In container haulage, the same logic applies from the pick-up point onwards: collecting the container from the port, the journey and delivery are separate stages, each shown with its own timestamp. You can share the tracking link with your customer, who can see for themselves whether the container is still at the port or on its way.

How do I share tracking with my own customer?

Tracking information does not stay only on your screen. Enter the customer's email address on the job and they will receive the tracking link, or send the link yourself. The customer sees the stages for themselves and does not call to ask where the load is.

Tracking without an email chain

Traditionally, the chain works like this: the shipper calls you, you call the driver and the information travels back by phone. When the driver confirms the stages in the app, the information appears on the tracking page without anyone having to pass it on by hand.

When your customer's customer also wants to track

If you haul for a freight forwarder or a larger haulier, their customer may also want to see the status of the transport. The shipper can forward the tracking link. Whoever opens the link sees only this transport, not the rest of your fleet or your other jobs. Remember that the link works for anyone it is forwarded to, so share it only with those who are meant to see the transport details.

What do I do if tracking does not update?

The most common causes and quick fixes

Most gaps are caused by one of three things: the driver has not yet confirmed the stage, the driver's phone has no network connection, or the vehicle's tracking device has not sent its position. First check the job's stages: if the load has been confirmed as loaded but the arrival estimate is not updating, the cause is usually the tracking device or its connection, and the estimate is then based on the route plan. The driver app stores confirmations even without a network and sends them when the connection returns, so a short dead zone does not interrupt tracking.

When to contact the driver

Call the driver if a stage has not updated as expected or the customer is already asking about the load. Ask for the sign-off and photos as soon as they arrive, so invoicing is not held up.

What does tracking cost, and how does it fit with the rest of transport management?

Per-vehicle pricing

RAHTIS is priced per vehicle, not per user: the first vehicle is free, and each additional vehicle that has run jobs during the month costs €14.90 a month (excl. VAT). Drivers use the app at no extra charge, and the tracking link is included in the price. An idle vehicle costs nothing, and no percentage is charged on jobs. For fleets of 100 vehicles or more, the price is agreed by quotation.

Tracking as part of the whole workflow

Tracking is not a separate add-on but part of the same job: entry, loading, transit, any swap, delivery and sign-off. Once the sign-off has been saved, you can invoice your own customer for the job and track payment status in the same place. The information flows from order to payment without tracking data having to be copied separately for the customer or the accountant.

FAQ

Can my customer see the tracking without their own login?

Yes. The customer opens the tracking page from the link without logging in. The page shows the stages with timestamps, the estimated time of arrival and, after delivery, the proof of delivery. The link can be forwarded, and whoever opens it sees only this transport.

Is the vehicle shown on a map all the time?

No. The tracking page has no map of the vehicle's position. If a GPS tracking system is connected to the vehicle, its latest position is used to calculate the arrival estimate, and the page shows when the estimate was last updated. Without a tracking device, the estimate is based on the route plan or the time given by the haulier.

Does tracking also work for transports in Sweden or the Baltics?

Yes. The stages and the tracking link work for international transports too, because they are based on the driver's confirmations. Traffic and road weather information is shown only for Finnish roads. RAHTIS works in ten languages, so you can share the tracking page with the customer in their own language.

Does the customer get the proof of delivery with the invoice or separately?

The customer can see the consignment note, the name of the person who signed and the delivery point photos on the tracking page immediately after delivery. When you create the invoice, the sign-off and the consignment note are already on the same job, so there is no need to dig out PDFs or WhatsApp photos.

Can I track several loads in the same view?

Yes. You see all jobs in progress and their stages in the same view, so you know at once what is in transit, what is at a swap point and what is awaiting sign-off. Delay and standstill alerts tell you which job to deal with first.

odotusajan-kirjaus-satulastauksessa-kulj.title: Recording waiting time during trailer swaps: a guide for drivers
odotusajan-kirjaus-satulastauksessa-kulj.description: Recording waiting time during trailer swaps: required fields, sample entries and tips to make the record stand up to payroll checks and inspection.
odotusajan-kirjaus-satulastauksessa-kulj.html:
Key takeaways

  • Waiting during a trailer swap is working time when the driver has to stay on site at the employer's disposal; if they are free to leave the truck, it is availability or waiting time that does not count as working time.
  • An accepted entry includes the start and end time, the location, the type of task and a reference such as the consignment note number.
  • The most common reasons for rejection are a missing vehicle registration, vague timings, no reason given, a conflict with the digital tachograph and a late retrospective entry.
  • Record waiting time for the same period as the digital tachograph records it, and attach a time-stamped photo of the consignment note.
  • The same driver entry serves both as working time for payroll and as the basis for a surcharge on the freight invoice.

The driver records waiting time during a trailer swap as working time by noting the start and end time, the location of the terminal or port, the nature of the task (trailer swap, container swap or waiting for the load) and a reference such as the consignment note number. This guide shows step by step how to make the entry, what a sample entry that stands up to payroll and working time inspection looks like, and on what grounds a waiting time entry is rejected. Recording waiting time during trailer swaps is closely regulated, and done properly it protects both the driver's pay and the employer's invoicing.

When is waiting time during a trailer swap working time?

Often, but not always. When a driver is swapping a trailer or container at a terminal or port and has to wait for loading, unloading or for the replacement unit to become available, the wait is working time if they have to stay on site at the employer's disposal, even though the vehicle is not moving and the driver is not doing physical work. Under section 3 of the Finnish Working Hours Act (872/2019), working time is time spent working and time during which the employee is obliged to be present at the workplace at the employer's disposal (Finnish Occupational Safety and Health Administration). The collective agreement for the truck sector makes this more specific: if the driver has to move the truck repeatedly on the orders of the loader or unloader, the time is working time, but if they are free to leave the truck, the wait is paid as waiting-time pay and does not count as working time (section 11, point 12).

The practical significance of this rule is considerable. If the driver has stayed at the terminal for their daily rest but is woken in the middle of it to move the truck when the trailer becomes available, that rest is no longer uninterrupted. The rest period is then broken and cannot count as daily rest, and the driver is back on working time. This means that recording waiting time during trailer swaps is not a mere formality: it determines whether the rest is considered complete or not. Without an entry, the driver and the employer risk misreading the situation and breaching the working time rules.

When waiting time counts as working time and when it does not

Waiting counts as working time when the trailer swap is part of a task assigned by the employer and the driver has to stay on site. If, on the other hand, the driver waits at the terminal on their own initiative without an assignment, or is outside working hours, the time is not recorded. In borderline cases, what matters is whether the driver had to stay on site or was free to use their time as they wished. The entry can be made by hand or per vehicle in a system such as RAHTIS, where the stages of a job run from the driver all the way to invoicing.

In practice the difference is clear: if the transport planner has told the driver to go to the terminal and wait for a trailer swap, the waiting is working time from the outset. If, instead, the driver decides to stop at the terminal to wait for the next job without any specific instruction, the time cannot be recorded as working time. Likewise, if the driver has said they are reachable but is free to leave the vehicle and use their own time, this is a period of availability, which does not count as working time, even though it may be paid for.

What information must a waiting time entry include?

A rejected waiting time entry is almost always an incomplete one: it lacks the time, the place or the reason. The payroll administrator cannot accept a line saying "at terminal 2 h", because it does not show whether it was waiting for a trailer swap or some other delay.

To make the entry complete, the driver needs to know exactly which fields the payroll administrator and the inspector expect to see. The table below lists the required fields; if any is missing, the entry is rejected automatically. These fields must be filled in for every waiting time entry, whether a paper form, email or a transport management system is used.

Required fields

FieldExample
Start date and time14/3 at 09:15
End time14/3 at 11:40
LocationTerminal, street address or port
TaskTrailer swap: changing trailers
Order or job referenceReference to the consignment note or CMR consignment note

Supporting details that speed up approval

A screenshot or time-stamped photo of the consignment note shortens the back-and-forth, as does the name of the consignee or the terminal supervisor. If the wait was caused by a queue, record your arrival time and the time your turn came separately. When the driver records these straight away during the job, the transport planner does not have to fill in details afterwards, and the entry goes to payroll and invoicing as it stands. In RAHTIS the driver confirms arrival and completion of the stop on their phone, and the entries and photos are sent even from areas without coverage as soon as the connection returns: see rahtis.eu/et.

Step by step: how the driver records waiting time during a trailer swap

Before arriving at the terminal

Record a time stamp as soon as you set off: take a photo or send a message on your phone showing your departure time and estimated arrival time at the terminal. Make sure the job instructions or consignment note include the customer's contact details so you can report a delay or an early arrival. If the load or trailer is not ready as agreed, report it before you arrive, so the reason for the wait can be verified from the start.

On arrival and when the wait begins

On arrival, record two things: the time and the place. In practice a time-stamped photo of the gate display, the gate sign or the yard, or a location-based entry in the app, is enough. Also record who is receiving you: the terminal name, gate number and any acknowledgement of your arrival. Tell reception you have arrived and ask them to confirm that the load or trailer is not ready, because it is exactly this confirmation that separates an accepted waiting time entry from a rejected one.

Directive 2002/15/EC distinguishes between working time and periods of availability. Waiting for loading or unloading also counts as working time when the driver has to stay at their workstation and the foreseeable duration of the wait is not known in advance. A period of availability, which does not count as working time, is a wait during which the driver is not required to remain at their workstation and whose foreseeable duration is known in advance (Article 3 of the directive on EUR-Lex). So record the start of the wait as soon as reception tells you the load is not there, and note whether you were told in advance how long the wait would be: do not wait to see whether it sorts itself out within the hour. Try recording waiting time in RAHTIS yourself: https://www.rahtis.eu/sv.

When the wait ends and recording what follows

Once the trailer has been swapped or the load secured, note the end time of the wait and continue the journey on the same entry. Finally, record the trailer or container number, the consignment note number and any acknowledgement from reception. The entry then forms a continuous chain: arrival, start of waiting, end of waiting and onward journey, all on the same job.

Sample entries: a trailer swap and waiting for a load

Example 1: trailer swap in the terminal yard

An accepted entry might look like this: "10/3, 09:15–10:40, trailer swap, terminal yard, Vantaa. Trailer change: empty trailer collected from the yard, loaded trailer dropped in its place, tractor unit and trailer recoupled. Witness: terminal shift supervisor." Record the time of arrival, not just the time the swap started.

Example 2: waiting at the gate before collecting a container

Another example: "10/3, 12:00 arrived at port gate, collection from the gate began at 13:30, container secured at 14:10. Reason for waiting: container had not yet been grounded." Here the waiting time spent at the gate is 1 h 30 min, and the entry shows the reason, so the person invoicing can claim compensation from the customer.

In both cases it is worth attaching a time-stamped photo of the gate display or the consignment note. When the same entry feeds directly into the job stages in RAHTIS, the driver does not copy information by hand, and the payroll administrator sees the waiting time in the same view as the rest of the job's records (https://www.rahtis.eu/lv).

The most common reasons for rejection in payroll

The most common reason for rejection is a missing vehicle or trailer registration: without a registration number, the payroll administrator cannot match the entry to the driving log record. The second is vague timing, such as just "all morning" with no start and end time. The third is a missing reason: an entry that only says "waiting terminal" does not show whether it was queuing because the load was being prepared or getting ready for the trailer swap.

The fourth reason is a conflict with the digital tachograph. If the tachograph shows rest for the same period for which the driver is claiming waiting time as working time, the payroll administrator will reject the entry unless it is a precisely defined exception. Working time is supervised by the occupational safety and health authority (since the start of 2026, the Finnish Licensing and Supervision Agency), and driving and rest times by the police at roadside checks. In either kind of inspection, discrepancies between the working time records and the tachograph must be explainable, so it is worth adding an explanation when the entry is made.

The fifth reason is a late retrospective entry made weeks afterwards. Avoid all five by recording the waiting time on the same day and adding the trailer swap details: terminal, container number and customer name. In RAHTIS the same entry is attached directly to the job, so invoicing and payroll see the same information without a separate email.

How does the entry stand up to a working time inspection?

The authorities compare waiting time entries with two sources: the driver's working time records and the vehicle's digital tachograph. Questions arise if the tachograph shows a stop during the trailer swap but nothing has been entered in the working time records, or the recorded time differs from the tachograph by hours.

Reconciling the digital tachograph and the manual entry

Record waiting time for the same period as the digital tachograph records. If the trailer swap started at 10:15 and ended at 12:45, the same times go into the working time records, not rounded hours. Explain in the entry why the vehicle was stationary: for example "queuing at terminal, container swap, collecting consignment note".

If the entry and the tachograph do not match, correct both on the same day and record the reason for the correction. Entries rejected in payroll are often ones where the driver's paper note and the system's time stamps differ with no explanation. When the entry, the tachograph and the payroll records tell the same story, the inspection goes through without questions.

The inspector may also ask for evidence that the wait was caused by the customer or the terminal and not by the driver's own delay. That is why photos of gate displays, emails from the sender or terminal receipts are worth their weight in gold. If the waiting time was interrupted by a break or rest, the inspector will want to see that the break was taken in accordance with the rules and that there are no gaps in the working time records. From the inspector's point of view, recording waiting time during trailer swaps is most reliable when every stop is explained and the driving schedule is consistent from departure to destination.

How does the transport planner handle waiting time entries in payroll?

In a small firm, the transport planner and the payroll administrator are often the same person, so it pays to process a waiting time entry as soon as the driver's record comes in. First check that the entry has a start and end time, the name of the terminal or port and the reason for waiting. If any of these is missing, ask for it to be completed the same day, not at the end of the payroll run.

Waiting time in customer invoicing and the freight rate

On the pay side, waiting time is recorded either as working time or as waiting time under the collective agreement, according to the driver's employment contract and the sector's terms. On the invoicing side the basis is different: the transport contract sets out which waiting time is charged as a surcharge and on what basis, for example at an hourly rate after a period of free waiting time. So agree with the customer in advance when free waiting time ends and how waiting is documented; information on the sector's terms of carriage is available, for example, from the haulage operators' association (SKAL).

In practice, then, the same entry is used twice: as working time for payroll and as a surcharge on the freight invoice. When both are based on the same driver entry, the figures also match at inspection.

How does RAHTIS support recording and invoicing waiting time?

RAHTIS is built so that the driver confirms arrival at each stop and completion of the stop on their phone: time stamps, locations, photos and notes are saved in the same workflow that the shipper follows step by step. The entry does not stay on paper or in a separate app; the transport planner sees it immediately and it travels on with the job. Waiting time at a stop is counted from arrival to confirmation. When the job is completed, the waiting time details are part of the same package as the consignment note and the POD, so invoicing is based on saved records rather than memory. This removes the typical problem of waiting time only coming to light when someone asks about it after the invoice has gone out.

Where RAHTIS does not help (yet)

RAHTIS does not know your customer-specific waiting time terms, so check the basis for the surcharge in your own transport contract. Nor does the system replace the tachograph or your payroll system; it produces entries that you transfer to your own payroll.

FAQ

Does the customer pay for waiting time if the trailer swap is delayed for reasons on the terminal's side?

Often, yes, but the basis lies in the contract, not in the driver's entry. The transport contract usually sets a period of free waiting time, after which the right to a surcharge arises. Record the reason for the delay, the start and end time and the order reference, so that invoicing can base the surcharge on saved data rather than memory.

Is the digital tachograph enough as evidence of waiting time, or is a separate entry needed?

A separate entry is needed. The digital tachograph shows that the vehicle was stationary, but not the reason or the task. The inspector will have questions if the stop on the tachograph and the working time records do not match. Record the same times, the location, the type of swap and a reference to the consignment note, so that any discrepancy can be explained afterwards.

What do I do if the terminal will not give arrival or release times in writing?

Record the times yourself on the same day and add your own evidence: a time-stamped photo of the consignment note, the name of the consignee or terminal supervisor and the container number. If the wait was caused by a queue, note your arrival time and the time your turn came separately. These supporting details speed up approval even when the terminal confirms nothing in writing.

Is waiting time during a trailer swap recorded as working time for the driver of the vehicle or for the driver doing the swap?

The entry goes into the working time records of the driver who was at the employer's disposal during the wait. If the driver of the replacement vehicle waits on site as instructed, the time is their working time. What decides it is not the vehicle's registration number but who was instructed to be there and whose free time the wait restricted.

How much waiting time is paid to the driver in full, and when is it treated as a break?

No general limit for full payment can be given without an employment contract or the sector's terms: on the pay side, your own contract terms decide. On the tachograph, a long stationary period is easily recorded as rest, so that the working time claim and the tachograph data conflict. Record the start and end of the wait accurately and explain in the entry in advance how breaks fit in.

pienen-kuljetusfirman-ajopaivakirja-sahk.title: An electronic driving log for a small haulage firm's drivers
pienen-kuljetusfirman-ajopaivakirja-sahk.description: An electronic driving log for a small haulage firm's drivers: up and running in six weeks, with data going straight to invoicing and no IT budget.
pienen-kuljetusfirman-ajopaivakirja-sahk.html:
Key takeaways

  • The law does not require paper: an electronic driving log is acceptable as long as the data is complete, reliable and can be checked afterwards.
  • A realistic budget for a firm with 1–10 vehicles is from tens to hundreds of euros a month, and per-vehicle pricing is usually the fairest model.
  • The logging app must work offline, open with a single tap and take less than a minute, or paper will be back in the cab.
  • Six weeks is enough to move from paper to electronic: selection and pilot, two weeks of running both in parallel, then retiring paper.
  • The same electronic entry serves the driving log, the consignment note, invoicing and payroll without copying.

A small haulage firm introduces an electronic driving log by choosing a phone-based logging app, making sure the data meets the statutory requirements, training drivers to log their own journeys and linking the data directly to invoicing and payroll. This guide shows step by step how a firm with 1–12 lorries makes the switch without an IT budget and without finally ditching paper until the electronic version has been proven to work.

Why should a small haulage firm digitise its driving log?

When you are the firm's transport planner, bookkeeper and safety manager all at once, every paper driving log is work you will have to sort out yourself later. An electronic driving log moves the recording to the driver at the moment the journey happens, and the data is ready at the same time for invoicing, payroll and working time monitoring.

Where the paper log breaks down in practice

On paper the handwriting is illegible, hours are missing or the sheet stays in the cab for a week. The requirements for drivers' logs and working time records are laid down in law, and the Finnish Ministry of Economic Affairs and Employment's guidance on working hours requires that the data can be verified afterwards. When the paper is poor, you end up correcting it in the evenings.

Time saved by linking dispatch and invoicing

When journeys, consignment note data and paid hours live in the same system, you do not copy anything twice. RAHTIS (rahtis.eu/fi) combines job tracking, driver shifts and payment tracking for invoices in one place, so the invoice can be made out from the recorded journeys instead of a paper log. The driver report also serves payroll without a separate home-made Excel set-up.

What does the law require of a driving log, and is an electronic version accepted?

Working time legislation and the driver's log

Driving and rest times are recorded by the vehicle's tachograph and on the driver card, but the employer must also keep working time records, which also cover work other than driving, such as loading and waiting. The driving log supplements this: it documents the route, load and mode of transport of each individual job. The law does not specify whether records are kept on paper or electronically, as long as the data is complete, reliable and can be checked afterwards. An electronic driving log is therefore acceptable if it produces the same information as the paper version.

Evidential value and archiving of electronic data

Evidential value is decisive in disputes: a customer questions the delivery time or a shipper questions the content of the consignment note. An electronic log contains a time stamp, the driver's identifier and an unalterable history, which is clearer evidence than paper. Retention obligations are worth checking with your own accountant, but in practice the data has to be kept on file for several years. In RAHTIS the journey data, consignment note and POD are linked to the same job, so the evidence is in one place rather than in separate folders (https://www.rahtis.eu/et). Remember that it must also be possible to show the driver's signature and the vehicle identifier afterwards.

What does an electronic driving log cost a small firm?

A realistic budget for a firm with 1–10 vehicles is from tens to hundreds of euros a month. The cost is made up of the software licence, the drivers' phones and your own time: installation, training and changing habits often cost more than the licences.

Pricing models: per vehicle, per user, fixed

ModelYou payBest suited toRisk
Per vehicleFixed sum / lorry / monthPredictable cost when drivers changeIdle months still cost money if the fleet shrinks
Per userSum / user / monthSmall fleet, many people loggingCost rises as you take on more staff
Fixed packageContract price / monthEstablished fleet and staffOversized if the firm shrinks

In a small firm, per vehicle is usually the fairest: the fleet is what earns the money. RAHTIS pricing follows this principle and suits firms from a single lorry upwards (https://www.rahtis.eu/lv).

Hidden costs: training, devices, integrations

Three items are often left out of the budget. Training drivers takes working days, and every new person logging needs to be inducted again. Devices: if logging is done on the driver's own phone, the cost is zero; company tablets cost €200–400 each. Integrations with invoicing and payroll are free when built in, but expensive when custom-made.

Remember the archiving obligation too: under Article 10 of Regulation (EC) No 561/2006 on driving and rest times, tachograph and driver card data must be downloaded regularly (the driver card at least every 28 days and the vehicle unit every 90 days, Commission Regulation (EU) No 581/2010) and kept for at least 12 months, and under Directive 2002/15/EC working time records must be kept for at least two years. So choose a service you can also get your data out of after the contract ends (EU Regulation 561/2006, EUR-Lex).

How do you choose an electronic driving log without an IT department?

Selection criteria for a small firm

When you are the transport planner, invoicing clerk and safety manager yourself, choose a solution against five criteria: can you use it on a phone without training, do you see entries in real time, does the data go straight to invoicing, does it work without a separate server, and is the pricing per vehicle rather than per user? Test each candidate on one real job, not a demo: log one loose trailer move, one consignment note and one empty run from start to finish. If installation needs a consultant or hours of learning, give it a miss.

Where RAHTIS meets these criteria and where it does not

RAHTIS is designed for firms from a single lorry upwards: the driver logs the shift and the stages of each job on a phone, and the same data is visible to you and ready for invoicing without copying from paper. Combining its own offer desk with transport management removes separate logins and paper notes about who owes what. You can apply at https://www.rahtis.eu/sv/apply.

To be honest: RAHTIS does not replace the statutory tachograph and driver card data or their download, and it is not a fleet maintenance system. If all you need is software to download and archive tachograph data, other tools will do.

How do you get drivers on board with the new way of logging journeys?

Mobile logging that copes with terminal routines

Logging is done on a phone, with gloves on, dirty screens and a poor signal. The solution must work offline, open with a single tap and ask only for the essential fields: origin, destination, load and job status. If logging takes more than a minute, it will not get done and paper will go back in the pocket.

Allow drivers their own way of working too: one logs at every stop, another at the end of the day. What matters most is that the data is created out on the road, not afterwards in the office from memory.

Ground rules for the transition period

Run both in parallel for two weeks: paper and electronic logging at the same time. This gives you comparison data and drivers learn without pressure. Agree on one rule: notes may be written on paper, but the official record is electronic, and missing entries are sorted out the same day, not a week later.

Remember the archiving obligation: in Finland electronic documents must be kept for the period laid down in the Accounting Act, and their evidential value requires the data to be unalterable and traceable (Vero.fi, the Finnish Tax Administration, on keeping electronic records). Once logging is in order, the same data is ready in RAHTIS for invoicing, and you can look for jobs for free vehicles on the RAHTIS offer desk; you can join via the application page.

How does driving log data get to invoicing and payroll?

Journey data to the consignment note and the invoice

When journey logging is electronic, the same entry can work in three places: as the driver's log, as an attachment to the consignment note and as the basis for invoicing. In practice the driver logs the job, the kilometres and waiting times, and the system links them to the order. In RAHTIS the consignment note and journey data are in the same workflow, so the invoice can be raised directly from the logged journey without copying from paper into Excel.

An honest limitation: RAHTIS does not send freight invoices through an e-invoicing operator. You make out the invoice in your own invoicing or financial management software and mark it on the job in RAHTIS, where the payment status and reminders are then handled. That is still quicker than typing it up from paper notes.

Working time and payroll

The same entry also works as a working time report. The driver's journeys, breaks and other work are saved with time stamps, and at the end of the month you send a ready-made report to payroll instead of a stack of paper slips. Digital logging is also more accurate: checks based on the vehicle's speed data reveal missing entries that on paper only come to light at inspection.

If you use separate payroll software, check before choosing which file format you can use to transfer working time data into it.

How do you move from paper to electronic step by step?

Six weeks is enough if the job is split into three two-week blocks: selection and pilot, parallel running and finally retiring paper. The aim is that no job goes unlogged by falling into a gap between the two systems during the transition.

Weeks 1–2: selection and pilot

Choose a solution using the criteria described earlier and put one driver on trial. Only one lorry's journeys are logged electronically; paper is not removed yet. At the same time, check the guidance from the industry association SKAL so the data you record is correct from the start: keeping a driving log. In week 2, go over with the pilot driver what worked and what felt like pointless tapping.

Weeks 3–4: parallel running

All vehicles now log both on paper and electronically. This is the most time-consuming phase, but it exposes the situations where the app does not fit the real work: waiting for loading, no signal in the yard, the change of day falling in the middle of a job. Compare the paper and electronic versions daily and fix logging habits immediately rather than collecting corrections on a list.

Weeks 5–6: retiring paper for good

The paper version stays in the vehicle as a backup, but it is no longer filled in. Drivers log only electronically, and you check the entries at the end of the day before invoicing. Once two full weeks have gone by with no missing entries and invoices have been produced from the driving log data without any separate reconciling, paper can be dropped completely. Keep one completed paper form as a reference point in case the tax authority or an inspector asks questions later.

Summary: where to start today?

Pick one vehicle and one driver, and log next week electronically alongside paper. Check that the data flows straight from the consignment note to invoicing without retyping. If everything goes through, extend it to a second vehicle and drop paper altogether within a month.

RAHTIS is designed for exactly this: from a single lorry upwards, with dispatch, driver shifts and payment tracking for invoices in one place and no separate IT budget. Try it in practice and see whether it fits the way you run your jobs.

FAQ

Can the driving log still be kept on paper if drivers refuse to use a mobile app?

Yes, because the law does not prescribe the form of the records, as long as the data is complete and can be checked afterwards. Paper, however, requires constant correcting and chasing: illegible handwriting, missing hours and late forms end up being fixed by you. Two weeks of parallel running lowers the threshold, and most drivers get used to logging on a phone when it takes less than a minute and works offline.

Does an electronic driving log work without a signal at a terminal or abroad?

Yes, if you choose an app that logs offline and uploads the data later. The signal at terminals is often weak, so the log must open with a single tap and save locally on the phone. Test this during the pilot on one real job, not a demo: log one loose trailer move and one empty run from start to finish. If logging gets stuck waiting for a connection, paper will soon be back in the cab.

Does a small firm need separate driving log software, or is a TMS with logging built in enough?

A separate driving log program rarely makes sense for a firm with 1–12 lorries. It is enough for logging to be part of the same workflow as the consignment note and invoicing, so the same entry serves the driving log, the invoice and payroll without copying. Choose a solution against five criteria: phone use without training, real-time visibility, direct transfer to invoicing, no server, and per-vehicle pricing.

How long must driving log data be kept by law?

The retention period depends on the data. Under Regulation (EC) No 561/2006 on driving and rest times, data downloaded from the tachograph and driver card must be kept for at least 12 months; under Directive 2002/15/EC working time records must be kept for at least two years; and under the Finnish Accounting Act data used as invoicing vouchers must be kept for at least six years from the end of the year in which the financial year ended. Check your own situation with your accountant, and before choosing, make sure you can get all your data out of the service even after the contract ends, so that the archiving obligation does not depend on the app.

How are incorrect entries made by drivers corrected afterwards?

Agree a rule that missing or wrongly logged journeys are sorted out the same day, not a week later. In a good system a correction leaves a time-stamped trace in the unalterable history, which preserves the evidential value of the records in a dispute. Check the entries yourself at the end of the day before invoicing, so errors do not make it onto the invoice and the driver gets feedback straight away.

proof-of-delivery-pod-rahtikiistat.title: Proof of delivery: how a POD protects your money in freight disputes
proof-of-delivery-pod-rahtikiistat.description: Proof of delivery (POD) proves a delivery with a signature, photo, time and location. How to avoid freight disputes and get paid faster.
proof-of-delivery-pod-rahtikiistat.html:
Key takeaways

  • Proof of delivery (POD) shows that the goods arrived: a signature, a photo, the time and location, or a barcode scan.
  • The right form of POD depends on the freight: for palletised loads, a signature and notes of any discrepancies; for trailer and container swaps, time, location and photos; for parcels and small consignments, a barcode or photo.
  • A digital POD is strong evidence when it contains a time and place recorded by the system, an identifiable signatory and storage that cannot be altered afterwards.
  • Send the POD with the invoice, and the most common reason for late payment, a missing delivery document, disappears.
  • In RAHTIS, the first vehicle is free and each additional vehicle that has run jobs costs €14.90 a month (excl. VAT); proof of delivery, photos and invoice status are in the same service.

Proof of delivery (POD) is a document or set of data that proves the goods were delivered as agreed: a signature, a photo, the time and location, or a barcode scan. Without it, unpaid freight comes down to your word against the customer's, and a slip of paper is easily lost. This article shows which form of POD suits which type of freight, from pallets to containers, and how to get paid faster.

What is proof of delivery, and why does it decide disputes over money?

Proof of delivery (POD) is evidence of delivery: it shows that the goods arrived, when, to whom and in what condition. In practice, it is a set of items collected by the driver, such as the consignee's signature, photos, the time and location of delivery or a barcode scan, which supports the invoice. In international road haulage, the consignee's signature on the CMR consignment note is the traditional POD.

The three jobs of a POD: delivery, receivable, evidence

A POD does three things at once. It closes the delivery, triggers invoicing and serves as evidence if the customer denies receiving the goods. Without a POD, the invoice rests on memory and trust.

Why a slip of paper is no longer enough

A slip of paper gets lost, gets wet or stays in the glovebox until the dispute is already a month old. A digital POD is saved at the moment of delivery with the time and location, so the evidence exists before anyone has a chance to question anything. The handling of delivery documents in RAHTIS is described in the terms of use.

Which forms of POD suit which type of freight?

The rule is simple: the POD must prove exactly what the dispute is about. With palletised freight, disputes are about quantity and condition; with swap units, about time and place; with parcels, about whether an individual item arrived. A summary below.

Type of freightPrimary PODWhy
Palletised freightSignature and notes of discrepanciesThe consignee counts and checks the pallets on site
Trailer swapTime, location and photos of the unit and sealThere is often nobody at the swap point to sign
ContainerTime, location, photos and seal numberCollection and return take place at terminals with no consignee present
Express and parcel freightBarcode scan or photoLarge numbers of items and time pressure require fast item-level proof

Palletised freight: signature and notes of discrepancies

A signature is still the strongest evidence when the consignee is present. Discrepancies, such as broken packaging, missing packages and water damage, are noted at the time of signing. If the consignee accepts the goods without reservations, in CMR carriage the goods are deemed, unless proven otherwise, to have been delivered in the condition described in the consignment note. Reservations about apparent damage must be made no later than at delivery, and about other damage in writing within seven days (Finnish Road Transport Contracts Act 345/1979, section 40, Finlex).

Trailer swaps and containers: time, location and photos

There is usually nobody at a swap yard or terminal gate to sign. The time and location recorded by the app show that the unit was at the agreed place at the agreed time, and photos of its sides and seal show its condition. That is enough for many disputes, because they are about time and place, not about the contents of the load.

Express and parcel freight: barcode and photo

A barcode scan shows that this particular item was delivered to this consignee. A photo serves as back-up for deliveries where the consignee is not present: the door, the address and the item in front of it. The combination stands up in a dispute where the consignee claims nothing arrived.

In the RAHTIS driver app, proof of delivery is the consignee's signature on the screen with their name, or a scanned consignment note, and in addition the driver takes photos of the unit, the seal and the load. The time and location are recorded for every confirmation. The app does not have barcode scanning (RAHTIS).

How does a digital POD protect you in a freight dispute?

What makes a POD usable as evidence

When a customer disputes a delivery, a slip of paper in a desk drawer is weak evidence: it may be hard to find, it does not always show the time or place, and the signature may be illegible. A digital POD is strong evidence when it contains three things: a time and place recorded by the system itself, identifiable details of the signatory, such as name and signature, and storage that cannot be altered afterwards. The same idea underlies the CMR consignment note: under Article 9 of the Convention, the consignment note is prima facie evidence of the contract of carriage, its conditions and the receipt of the goods.

Typical disputes and missing evidence

Three disputes keep recurring in a small firm. The customer says the delivery never came, even though the driver unloaded the goods. The customer claims damage that nobody photographed during unloading. Or the consignee recorded a different quantity from the consignment note, and the only evidence is the driver's recollection from a week ago.

A digital POD helps in all of them in the same way: a photo of the damage with time and place, the consignee's signature on the phone screen, and everything saved against this particular transport. When you receive a complaint, you reply with a single message containing the photos, signature, time and place. Many disputes end there, because the other side can see you are not guessing. If the matter goes to debt collection or to court, evidence that is timestamped and tied to a location is much stronger than a slip of paper.

Checklist: what to do when a customer does not pay?

Before delivery

Agree the freight rate, payment terms and late payment interest in writing. Between businesses, under the Finnish Interest Act, late payment interest is the reference rate plus eight percentage points, unless otherwise agreed. Make sure the loading list and delivery address match the order. If the load is out of the ordinary, for example wet, fragile or requiring special unloading, record it before departure.

At the time of delivery

The driver collects a POD suited to the freight: signature and photos for palletised freight; time, location and photos of the trailer or container. Discrepancies are recorded immediately on the consignment note and in photos, not afterwards. If the consignee refuses to sign, the driver records the refusal, the time and the place, and reports it to the office straight away. Never leave the site without any evidence.

When a dispute flares up

Send the invoice and the POD together as soon as possible, preferably within 24 hours, because many disputes arise from paperwork arriving weeks late. Call before sending a payment reminder: many disputes are resolved when the customer's accounts payable clerk sees the signed POD. If payment still does not come, send a written payment reminder and then pass the debt to collection. Document every step: dates, calls and attachments. Without a POD you have an opinion; with a POD you have a document.

How does the POD connect to invoicing and tracking receivables?

The POD as an attachment to the invoice

When the POD is digital, it can be sent as an attachment to the invoice: consignment note, signature and photos in one package. The customer cannot claim they did not receive the delivery document, because it came with the invoice. This removes the most common cause of delay, where an invoice waits weeks for a "missing paper".

Tracking unpaid invoices without a paper memo

Once the delivery has been signed for, you know the transport is ready to invoice, and you can track the invoice up to the due date. You can see at a glance who owes you money and for how long, without a separate memo or spreadsheet.

In RAHTIS, the proof of delivery, photos and consignment note are on the same job, and the invoice status (open, overdue or paid) is visible in the same service. The shipper sees the arrivals, confirmations, photos and locations in the transport tracking, so delivery documents do not need to be sent separately.

What does a POD require of a driver who speaks another language, and of the phone?

A simple interface

For the driver, a POD must take just a few taps: take photos, ask for a signature, mark as done. In a team that speaks several languages, long text forms cause mistakes, so clear buttons and the driver's own language work better. The signature is drawn with a finger on the phone screen, and no paper needs to be scanned at the office afterwards. The driver should see only the details of their own task, in their own language, not the whole system.

Without a connection at ports and warehouses

At ports, warehouse yards and in remote areas, the signal often drops. A POD app must store the photo, time and location on the phone and send them automatically when the connection returns. If a confirmation is lost because of a network outage, that is exactly the load most likely to be disputed later. The RAHTIS driver app keeps entries in a queue when offline and sends them in order with the time of the tap, but it cannot make up for poor lighting: in the dark months, it is worth teaching drivers a fixed routine for taking photos.

How does RAHTIS handle POD, and what does it not do?

Job, proof of delivery and invoice in one chain

RAHTIS covers the transport from start to finish: the order is entered, the driver confirms arrival, takes photos and obtains proof of delivery (a signature or a scanned consignment note) on the phone, and everything is saved on the same job. When a customer questions a delivery, you show the job details, not a pile of paper. Invoice status is visible in the same service, so tracking receivables does not depend on a sticky note.

Honest limitations: what RAHTIS does not replace

The RAHTIS load board is not as large a freight exchange as Trans.eu or TIMOCOM, and RAHTIS does not replace an accountant, an insurer or a lawyer in the legal phase of a freight dispute. A POD that is timestamped and tied to a location is evidence, not a verdict. If a dispute goes to debt collection, you will need the help of a collection agency or a lawyer. RAHTIS takes care of collecting the evidence and keeping it in order, so it can be found when it is needed.

How much does a digital POD cost, and is it worth it for a firm with 1–12 vehicles?

RAHTIS pricing: first vehicle free, additional vehicles €14.90 a month

In RAHTIS, the first vehicle is free, and each additional vehicle that has run jobs during the month costs €14.90 a month (excl. VAT). A vehicle standing in the workshop or up for sale costs nothing, and no percentage is charged on jobs. So with a fleet of four active vehicles, the total is 3 × €14.90 = €44.70 a month, including the driver app, proofs of delivery, photos and invoice tracking. The first month is free.

When the investment pays for itself

The benefit comes from three places. A single freight dispute that photos and a signature settle in your favour can cover the costs for a long time. Second, less paperwork and email frees up time for dispatch. Third, invoices go out faster when the proof of delivery is available straight away, and payments come in sooner. To be honest: if you only haul for regular customers who always pay on time, the benefit is smaller and depends mainly on whether you save hours of office work.

FAQ

Can a POD be sent by text message or email, or is an app needed?

You can send a POD by email or message, but then the photo stays in a message thread without a system-recorded time or a link to this particular transport. An app records the time, place and transport automatically. Email works as a fallback, not as the main method, because a broken chain of evidence weakens your position in a dispute.

How long must POD evidence be kept?

Under section 41 of the Finnish Road Transport Contracts Act and the CMR Convention, an action concerning carriage must be brought within one year, or within three years in cases of wilful misconduct or gross negligence. When the POD is attached to an invoice, it forms part of the accounting records, and under the Finnish Accounting Act vouchers must be kept for at least six years from the end of the year in which the financial year ended (Accounting Act 1336/1997, Finlex). The safest course is therefore to keep proofs of delivery for at least six years.

Does POD confirmation work without a connection, for example at a port or warehouse?

Yes, provided the app stores the photo, time and location on the phone and sends them automatically when the connection returns. It is precisely in places without a signal that confirmations are easily lost, and precisely those loads that are disputed later. Test how the app works offline before you rely on it.

What do I do if the customer disputes the consignee's signature?

Reply with a single message containing the full evidence package: the signature and the consignee's name, the time, the location and the photos. Because the system recorded the time and place itself at the moment of delivery, it is hard for the customer to justify the dispute. If the matter goes to debt collection, evidence that is timestamped and tied to a location is strong proof.

Is a digital POD also suitable for transports given to a subcontractor?

Yes, and it is especially useful then: when the subcontractor's driver confirms delivery in the same way, you have evidence even though the transport was not run with your own vehicle. You can show the customer that the delivery took place, and separate your own liability from the subcontractor's performance. Make a POD requirement a condition of the subcontracting agreement.

rahtikirjan-toimittaminen-asiakkaalle-sa.title: Sending the consignment note to the customer electronically
rahtikirjan-toimittaminen-asiakkaalle-sa.description: You can send a consignment note to your customer electronically as a PDF or as an e-CMR. Here is how delivery, signing and retention comply with Finnish law.
rahtikirjan-toimittaminen-asiakkaalle-sa.html:
Key takeaways

  • Electronic consignment notes are permitted in Finland: the Finnish Road Transport Contracts Act allows them for domestic carriage, and for international carriage the e-CMR is based on the Additional Protocol to the CMR Convention, which entered into force for Finland on 11 April 2019.
  • The e-CMR only works for carriage between countries that have acceded to the Additional Protocol, and not all EU countries have done so.
  • A PDF or photo sent by email is a copy of a paper consignment note, not an e-CMR; its evidential value in a dispute is weaker than that of a document signed within a system.
  • A consignment note attached to an invoice is part of the accounting records and, under the Finnish Accounting Act, must be kept for at least six years; the ten-year period applies to the financial statements and the books of account.
  • Start the switch with one customer and one route, not all jobs at once.

Yes, you can: a consignment note can be sent to the customer electronically, either as a PDF copy or as an electronic consignment note. For domestic carriage, electronic consignment notes are permitted under the Finnish Road Transport Contracts Act, and for international carriage the e-CMR is based on the Additional Protocol to the CMR Convention, administered by the United Nations Economic Commission for Europe (UNECE). This guide takes you through delivery step by step, signing and retention.

Can a consignment note be sent to the customer electronically?

Yes. For domestic carriage in Finland, issuing a consignment note is not even mandatory, and under a provision added to the Road Transport Contracts Act (345/1979) in 2019, a consignment note may also be issued electronically. In international road haulage, an electronic consignment note, or e-CMR, is possible when both the country of departure and the country of destination have acceded to the Additional Protocol to the CMR Convention.

The Additional Protocol to the CMR Convention permits electronic consignment notes

The Additional Protocol on the electronic consignment note was concluded in Geneva in 2008 and entered into force internationally in 2011. It entered into force for Finland on 11 April 2019. Countries that have acceded include Sweden, Norway, Denmark, Estonia, Germany and Poland, but not all EU countries, so check the destination country before you give up paper. The text of the Additional Protocol and the list of contracting states are available on the UNECE website.

When a PDF is enough and when you need an e-CMR

A PDF that you scan and email to the customer is in practice a copy of the paper: the signature is an image, and you cannot show that the document has not been altered. That is enough for many regular customers, but it is not an e-CMR. If the customer or consignee requires an e-CMR under the Additional Protocol, you need a dedicated e-CMR service. RAHTIS does not issue e-CMRs under the Additional Protocol: the driver takes the signature and photos in the app and attaches the scanned consignment note to the job, and after delivery the customer can see them via the tracking link.

PDF or e-CMR: what difference does it make when sending to the customer?

In short: a scanned or PDF consignment note is acceptable to many customers, but its evidential value in a dispute or an inspection is weaker than that of an e-CMR signed within a system. A PDF is a picture of a document; an e-CMR is the document itself, with its signatures and timestamps stored in the system.

PDF: quick, but weaker as evidence

If you photograph the paper consignment note and send the customer a PDF, delivery is quick. The problem is that a PDF does not reliably show when and by whom it was signed. If the customer disputes the delivery or payment is delayed, you will be relying on the paper original, so keep it.

e-CMR: signature and timestamp in the system

An e-CMR is an electronic consignment note under the Additional Protocol, signed by the parties to the contract of carriage within the system, with every change remaining visible together with its timestamp. The customer can see the signatures in the system immediately after unloading.

Comparison table: scanned paper, PDF, e-CMR

Scanned paperPDFe-CMR
SignatureBy hand on paperAs an image or none at allElectronically in the system
TimestampNot reliableNot reliableRecorded by the system
RetentionPaper + imageFileIn the system
Evidential value in a disputeThe paper original decidesWeakStrong

In RAHTIS, the image of the consignment note, the sign-off and the photos from the delivery point are stored on the job, and you can invoice your own customer from the same job. You can sign up for a trial at https://www.rahtis.eu/en/apply.

How do you send an electronic consignment note to the customer, step by step?

The process has four steps: issuing the consignment note, the driver's sign-off, delivery to the customer and attaching the proof of delivery (POD) to the invoice. Once the steps are in place, the same routine repeats on every job.

Step 1: issuing the consignment note before collection

Issue the consignment note before the lorry leaves for collection. Enter the consignor, consignee, goods details and agreed terms once; do not copy a paper template by hand. If the job is already in the system, the basic details are ready.

Step 2: the driver's sign-off at collection and delivery

The driver sees the job on their phone and confirms collection and delivery. The consignee signs for receipt on the driver's device, so the proof of delivery is created directly in the system.

Step 3: delivery channel – email, tracking link or e-CMR service

Choose the delivery channel according to what the customer accepts. A PDF sent by email is a copy of the paper: it is easy to read, but it is not an e-CMR. A genuine electronic consignment note is created in an e-CMR service, where the data are stored together with the signatures and every change is logged, so either party can show what the consignment note said and when it was confirmed. Large consignees, such as manufacturers and retail chains, may require an e-CMR; smaller ones are often content with a PDF. Find out from each regular customer what they accept, and do not run two parallel processes for the same job.

Step 4: attaching the proof of delivery to the invoice

Once delivery has been signed for, attach the consignment note and proof of delivery to the invoice. Under the Finnish Accounting Act (1336/1997), vouchers such as a sales invoice and its attachments must be kept for at least six years from the end of the year in which the financial year ended. In RAHTIS, the sign-off, photos and image of the consignment note are on the job, and the invoice created from the job goes to the customer as a PDF attachment.

What is required of an e-CMR system?

An e-CMR must be based on the Additional Protocol to the CMR Convention. Under the Additional Protocol, the parties authenticate the electronic consignment note with a reliable electronic signature linked to it, and the system must ensure that the document retains its integrity and cannot be altered without detection.

Signature and integrity

Each party, i.e. the consignor, the carrier and the consignee, confirms its own stage, and the system records who confirmed it and when. Once the consignment note has been confirmed, its content can no longer be changed without detection: corrections are shown separately. This is exactly what distinguishes an e-CMR from an ordinary PDF that anyone can edit.

Identifying the driver and the other parties

Identification determines whether a signature can be linked to the right person. The driver must log in to the system with their own credentials, not a shared company login. The same applies to the consignor and the consignee. In RAHTIS, each driver gets their own login, and the sign-off is recorded under the driver's name. You can send questions via https://www.rahtis.eu/en/apply.

How long must an electronic consignment note be kept?

Retention periods under the Accounting Act

Under Chapter 2, section 10 of the Finnish Accounting Act (1336/1997), vouchers must be kept for at least six years from the end of the year in which the financial year ended, and the financial statements and books of account for at least ten years from the end of the financial year. When a consignment note or proof of delivery is attached to a sales invoice, it forms part of the vouchers, so six years is the minimum. The format does not affect the retention period: the same applies to paper and electronic records. For claims arising under the contract of carriage, it may be sensible to keep the consignment note even longer.

Electronic archiving: legibility and integrity

Records kept electronically must remain legible, and printable if necessary, throughout the retention period, and the method of storage must be reliable. In practice this means a durable file format, backups and a system from which the document can still be retrieved years later. If your electronic archive is in a service provider's system, make sure you can export the records even after the contract ends.

What an audit-proof archive means

In practice, every transport document can be found by job or invoice number, with the consignment note, proof of delivery and invoice kept together. In RAHTIS, the job's sign-offs, photos and invoice can be found on the job, and you can track the invoice's payment status in the same place. You can apply to use RAHTIS on the website.

How does an electronic consignment note speed up invoicing in a small firm?

When the consignment note and sign-off are electronic, the proof of delivery does not stay in the driver's pocket or a paper folder. It is stored on the job at the time of delivery, and the invoice can be sent as soon as the load has been delivered. In a paper-based chain, the same cycle takes days or weeks.

Proof of delivery attached to the job

Each job is a self-contained record: consignment note, proof of delivery and agreed price in one place. When the sign-off comes in, it is linked directly to that job, and the invoice can be raised without a separate folder or digging through emails.

Who pays late, and why the document is missing

Late payment is often caused by a missing proof of delivery, not by unwillingness to pay. When the document is missing, chasing payment turns into an investigation: calls, emails and resending. With an electronic chain, you can see for yourself which jobs are missing a sign-off and sort it out before the due date.

What should you do in the first week of switching to electronic consignment notes?

Start with one customer and one route. Do not try to move all jobs at once: pick a regular customer, agree with them on electronic consignment notes and run the first job that way.

Checklist: customers, drivers, archiving

  • Agreement: make sure the customer accepts electronic delivery and in what format. For international carriage, check whether the destination country has acceded to the e-CMR Additional Protocol.
  • Drivers: install the app and try out the sign-off, signature and photos on one load.
  • Archiving: decide where the consignment note and proof of delivery are stored and how they are attached to the invoice.

Drivers who speak different languages

Choose a system whose driver app works in the driver's language. Test it yourself: if the sign-off and photos cannot be done without help, the language barrier eats up the minutes you saved. The RAHTIS driver app is available in ten languages.

How does RAHTIS handle delivery and archiving of consignment notes?

In RAHTIS, the job, the driver's sign-off and the invoice are in one place. Once the load has been delivered, the driver takes the consignee's signature and photos in the app and attaches an image of the consignment note to the job. The customer can see them via the tracking link, and the invoice created from the job is sent to the customer as a PDF attachment. You can track the invoice's payment status in the same system. RAHTIS does not issue e-CMRs under the Additional Protocol; if the customer requires one, you need a separate e-CMR service.

Jobs and their attachments remain searchable in the system, so the paper notebook and separate spreadsheets are no longer needed. However, the statutory duty to retain accounting records lies with the business itself, so make sure that invoices and their attachments also end up in your accounts.

RAHTIS is built for small haulage firms, from a single vehicle upwards. Pricing is per vehicle, not per user: the first vehicle is free, and each additional vehicle that has run jobs costs €14.90 a month (excl. VAT).

FAQ

Can I send the consignment note to the customer by WhatsApp or email?

You can, but then you are sending a copy, not an e-CMR. A copy is easy to read, but its origin and integrity are hard to prove after the event. Keep the original and ask each regular customer what they accept.

Is a photo of the consignment note taken by the driver acceptable?

A photo is a copy, just like a PDF sent by email. It is good everyday evidence of delivery, but it is not an e-CMR and does not replace the signed original. A genuine electronic consignment note is created in a system where the parties sign electronically and every change is logged.

How much does it cost a small haulage firm to introduce electronic consignment notes?

The cost depends on the service, so ask the provider for a price directly. In RAHTIS, the first vehicle is free and each additional vehicle that has run jobs costs €14.90 a month (excl. VAT); an e-CMR service has to be obtained separately. The real saving comes from faster invoicing and less chasing, because the proof of delivery no longer stays in the driver's pocket.

What do I do if a customer still insists on a paper consignment note?

Use paper for that customer and attach a photo to the job, but do not run two parallel processes for the same job. Find out your regular customers' requirements in the first week and start the switch with one customer and one route.

Is an electronic signature required, or is the driver's sign-off in the app enough?

It depends on what you need. As everyday proof of delivery, a sign-off made with the driver's own credentials plus the consignee's signature is often enough, because the system records who signed and when. An e-CMR under the Additional Protocol, however, requires a reliable electronic signature that identifies the signatory and is linked to the consignment note in such a way that any changes are detectable.

rahtilaskujen-hoito-ilman-jalkikaiteista.title: Freight invoicing without paperwork after the fact
rahtilaskujen-hoito-ilman-jalkikaiteista.description: Freight invoicing without paperwork after the fact: order, sign-off and POD travel in one chain, so the invoice can go out as soon as goods are delivered.
rahtilaskujen-hoito-ilman-jalkikaiteista.html:
Key takeaways

  • A paperless freight invoicing process relies on recording the job details once, with the same record flowing from the order to the consignment note, the driver's sign-off and the finished invoice.
  • An electronic freight invoice must contain the same mandatory details as a paper invoice, and in Finland invoices, as accounting vouchers, must be kept for at least six years from the end of the year in which the financial year ended.
  • The driver's mobile sign-off and the POD attachment are saved to the job at the moment of delivery, which does away with envelopes of receipts scanned after the fact and speeds up payment.
  • Freight exchange and loose trailer jobs fit into the same invoicing process when each customer receives its own invoice with its own terms and references.
  • RAHTIS does not replace accounting software: the balance sheet and annual accounts are still handled by your accountant.

You can handle freight invoices without paperwork after the fact when the consignment note details, the driver's sign-off and the POD attachment go straight from the system into the invoice: the order is created once, the driver signs off the job on a mobile and the invoice material is ready complete with attachments. This guide goes through the whole life cycle from order to archiving, including loose trailer and freight exchange jobs.

What does freight invoicing without paperwork after the fact mean?

A paperless freight invoicing process means that the job details are created once in the system and go straight from there into the invoice: the order, route, driver's sign-off, POD attachment and consignment note details in a single chain.
