All the invoice data is ready in one place, and you do not have to spend an evening going through envelopes of receipts and notes.

For a small business the benefit is tangible: when dispatching, invoicing and bookkeeping are all handled by the same person, every line typed by hand takes time that is lost elsewhere. According to the Finnish Tax Administration, an electronic invoice must contain the same mandatory details as a paper invoice, so the law does not force you to use paper (Finnish Tax Administration). In RAHTIS the shipper publishes the job once and the driver signs off each stage directly, so the invoice material is ready before the lorry is back at base. In practice the process starts with the customer's job or the freight exchange job being entered once, not in three places.

The essence of going paperless is not the technology itself but joining the information flows into a single chain in which the same data is never entered twice. When the driver signs off the delivery in the mobile app, the sign-off does not disappear into an inbox waiting for a separate invoicing round; from that moment all the invoice data is in one place, and you can make the invoice right away in your own invoicing software without re-typing anything. This means the invoice can be in the customer's inbox or online bank before the driver has even made it back home. With the traditional model this would be impossible, because invoicing always depends on the paper consignment note coming back and the data being entered into the system by hand. In a paperless process that delay disappears and the invoicing lead time shrinks from days to hours, which significantly improves the company's cash flow.

What requirements apply to an electronic freight invoice in Finland?

Mandatory invoice details

The Finnish VAT Act sets out what every freight invoice must contain: the names and details of the seller and the buyer, the Business ID or other identifier, the invoice number, the date, the date or period of supply, the quantity and nature of the goods or the extent and nature of the services, the VAT rate, the amount payable and the payment terms. Whether the job comes via a freight exchange or from your own customer, the same fields are filled in every time. In RAHTIS the order details (parties, route, price) and the consignment note details are already on the job, so you do not have to hunt for them on paper when making out the invoice. If you invoice abroad, for example a Swedish or German customer, the details are the same, but the language and references are worth checking at the order stage. You can try it out in practice at Application · RAHTIS.

In addition to the mandatory invoice details, the haulage sector has its own specific requirements that general invoicing software does not always cover. A freight invoice often includes a reference number linking it to a particular job or transport contract, plus a breakdown of surcharges such as waiting time, unloading delays or ADR surcharges. Itemising these by hand on a paper invoice or in general invoicing software is laborious and error-prone. When the source data comes straight from the transport management system, the breakdown can be taken directly from the prices agreed with the order and the extra events recorded during the transport. This reduces customers' questions about the content of the invoice and speeds up payment.

Archiving and retention period

Under the Finnish Accounting Act (1336/1997, chapter 2, section 10), vouchers such as invoices and other accounting material must be kept for at least six years from the end of the year in which the financial year ended, and the financial statements, the annual report and the books for at least ten years from the end of the financial year. Electronic archiving is permitted as long as the data remains unaltered and accessible throughout the retention period. In practice this means POD attachments, consignment note details and invoices can live in the same system without cardboard files. When the driver's sign-off and attachment have been linked to the job during the transport, archiving happens at the same time, and no one is left with paperwork after the fact.

For retention requirements, what matters is that the electronic archive is protected against changes and its data is traceable. The system must be able to show when the invoice was created, when the attachments were added and who signed them off. RAHTIS stores the time stamps of the job's events and who recorded them, so the audit trail is in order without a separate log book. If the tax authority asks for evidence of a particular job from three years ago, the material is in one place: the invoice entry, consignment note, POD attachment and the driver's sign-off with time stamps. In the paper world the same job might be scattered across three or four files in different offices, and some of the information could be missing or hard to read.

How do you get freight invoice data straight from the transport management system into the invoice?

Order stage: getting the job details right once

The chain starts with the order: the customer's email or a freight exchange job is turned into a transport task in the system, with the collection and delivery addresses, load description, freight rate, surcharges (such as waiting time or ADR) and payment terms. This data is saved once and reused at every stage: for the consignment note, the driver's task list and finally the invoice. Eliminating retyping is the core of the whole chain, because every line copied by hand is one more possible error on the invoice and one more reason for the customer to pay late.

In practice this means that when you enter a job in RAHTIS, the same record goes with it all the way: from the order to the consignment note details, the driver's sign-offs and on to the invoice. You do not have to dig the agreed price out of a notebook later or check scraps of paper, because everything is already in the same record. The system does not replace dispatching decisions; it simply makes sure that data entered once is not lost on its way to the invoice.

The quality of the data created at the order stage determines whether the whole chain works. If an address is incomplete or the freight rate is missing, these gaps carry through to the consignment note and the invoice, so the first entry has to be made carefully. In practice it pays to create order templates for different types of customer: a regular customer with fixed routes and prices, a freight exchange job where prices vary, and a one-off job where everything is entered by hand. Once the template is ready, the mandatory fields are filled in by default and only exceptions need manual input. This halves the time spent on orders and reduces the risk of entry errors, because the system will not let a job go forward without the mandatory details.

Consignment note details as the basis for the invoice

The consignment note (CMR) is filled in from the same record, and once the driver signs off the delivery and the POD attachment has been saved, all the invoice data is in one place and you can make the invoice right away in your own invoicing software, without re-typing anything. The invoice shows the customer details, freight rate, surcharges and attachments, all derived from the original order and the events of the transport. Retention obligations are best checked directly in official guidance, such as on the Finnish Tax Administration's website, so that archiving is done correctly from the start.

The consignment note details form the basis of the invoice because they contain what actually happened during the transport: loading and unloading times, any damage or discrepancies, and the consignee's acknowledgement. When this data comes straight from the system, the invoice is based not just on the order but on verifiable events. If the customer claims the delivery was late, the time stamp of unloading attached to the invoice shows when it actually happened. If the freight rate includes waiting time, the driver's sign-off verifies how long the wait lasted. This chain from order to consignment note to invoice is what makes freight invoicing without paperwork after the fact possible: every invoice line can be traced to a concrete event, not to a note or a receipt.

How are the driver's sign-offs and attachments added to a digital freight invoice?

POD and CMR sign-off on mobile

Straight after unloading, the driver photographs the signed CMR or consignment note on their phone and marks the load as delivered in the app. The photo, time stamp and location are saved directly to that job, so paper copies do not have to be posted back or scanned at the office in the evening. If the consignee insists on a paper acknowledgement, a photographed document is enough as an invoice attachment for most customers.

How easy the driver's mobile app is to use determines how likely the sign-off is to be done correctly and on time. If the app is slow or needs lots of fields filled in, the driver puts the sign-off off until the evening or forgets it altogether, and invoicing is delayed. The RAHTIS mobile sign-off is designed around the bare minimum: the job opens, the driver takes a photo, the consignee signs on the screen and the job is marked as complete. The location and time stamp are saved in the background with no extra step. This means the sign-off is done before the driver starts the engine at the delivery point, and the invoice material is ready straight away.

Automatically linking attachments to the job

When the job is marked as complete, the POD photo, the CMR sign-off and any other attachments are in the same record that the invoice is based on. The invoicing software does not have to ask for attachments separately afterwards, and they do not need to be attached by hand via email. In RAHTIS the driver's sign-off is visible to the customer step by step, and the signed CMR and unloading photos are saved to the job, where the customer can see them (https://www.rahtis.eu/lt). This removes the most common reason for late payment: the customer cannot claim that the delivery document is missing.

An honest limitation: if the customer requires the original paper CMR to be posted, a digital image only partly replaces it, and the original must still be kept.

Linking the attachments to the job means in practice that the invoice is not a stand-alone document but is based on the job record. When the invoice goes to the customer, the POD attachment, the CMR photo and any additional explanations go with it, without anyone having to put them together separately. This is a significant difference from the traditional model, where invoicing is a separate step that needs its own attachments, its own email and its own archiving. In RAHTIS these are all part of the same job: when you mark the invoice you have sent on the job, the supporting material is already in place and does not have to be put together separately.

How do loose trailer and freight exchange jobs fit into the same invoicing process?

Loose trailer work should not be a separate invoicing channel. When freight exchange jobs and your own customers go through the same system, filling empty legs and invoicing are handled without a notebook or CMR copies sent by post.

Freight exchange job details straight into the system

When you take a job from a freight exchange, the customer details, route and freight are entered once, not afterwards from a receipt. In RAHTIS the driver signs off collection and delivery, and the POD attachment and a photo of the consignment note are saved with the job. An electronic consignment note (e-CMR) can be used under the Additional Protocol to the CMR Convention only if both the country of departure and the country of destination are parties to the Protocol (UNECE e-CMR page). Finland is a party, but not all EU countries are, and an e-CMR is issued in a service designed for that purpose. The photo and on-screen sign-off stored in RAHTIS are not an e-CMR, so the paper CMR still travels with the goods.

The catch with loose trailer jobs is that customers change and invoice terms vary: one pays at 14 days, another at 30 days, a third requires its own reference number system. When this information is recorded with the job, you see each customer's terms right on the job when you make the invoice, without having to remember who pays on which terms. This is particularly important when you run a mix of jobs: your own customers, jobs from Trans.eu and jobs agreed directly by phone, all in the same week. If invoicing is a separate process, you have to check each job's terms individually, which takes longer than the driving itself.

Invoicing several customers

Each customer receives its own invoice with its own terms and references, even if the jobs are in the same calendar. When the POD and consignment note are already attached, the invoice can be sent as soon as the goods are delivered, and a later empty leg that gets filled is handled in the same way. RAHTIS handles both the same way; more information and application: Application · RAHTIS.

Managing several customers requires the system to keep jobs clearly apart: who ordered it, what the route is, what the price is and when the invoice falls due. When this information is in the same calendar, you can see at a glance which invoices have been sent and which are waiting. This prevents double invoicing and forgotten jobs, which are the most common mistakes in a paper-based process. And when filling empty legs is part of the same system, invoicing the return load follows the same logic: the driver signs off collection and delivery, the POD is saved to the job and the invoice is made out on that basis.

How are archiving and inspections handled without a paper archive?

When freight invoice data, the driver's sign-offs and POD attachments build up in the same system, the archive creates itself as you work. Every job remains searchable: the consignment note details, attachments and invoice can be found by customer or registration number in seconds, with no safe or old files.

Payment tracking without a notebook

You can see the status of each invoice directly in the system: sent, paid, overdue. Instead of recording "who owes what" in a paper notebook, you mark the invoice you have sent on the job, and RAHTIS tracks due dates job by job and flags the overdue ones. Payment reminders go out without a separate Excel file, and you no longer have to collect scraps of paper for your accountant.

Effective payment tracking depends on the system knowing the status of every invoice in real time. When you mark the invoice as sent, it is open. When payment arrives, it changes to "paid". If the due date passes, the status changes to "overdue" and the system flags it without you having to go through a list by hand. This is a significant advantage over Excel-based tracking, where the status has to be updated by hand and overdue invoices can go unnoticed for weeks. In RAHTIS overdue invoices are shown with their status, and if an invoice has not been marked as paid, RAHTIS sends the customer a free payment reminder on your behalf the day after the due date and again seven days later, without you having to look up the original invoice or the customer's contact details.

Responding to inspections from a digital archive

When the tax authority or customs asks for documents, digging through years-old piles of paper becomes a search. You select the period and the customer, and the system lists the consignment notes, POD attachments and invoices. The same applies to disputes with customers: if the other party claims a delivery is missing, the sign-off time stamp and the POD attachment can be shown in moments. RAHTIS keeps the archive in order automatically, but final responsibility for retention obligations and tax treatment lies with you and your accountant, as with any system.

In an inspection, speed and completeness are what count. If the tax authority gives you a week to supply invoices and related documents for a three-month period, putting them together from a paper archive can take a whole day. From a digital archive the same material is put together in minutes: you select the period, filter by customer and the system lists everything, including attachments. This not only saves time but also reduces the risk of errors, because documents can get lost or mixed up when gathered by hand. What is more, the digital archive is always in the same format and in the same place, so responding to different inspectors' requests is consistent and quick.

What should you bear in mind when moving from paper to electronic freight invoices?

Making the switch in 30 days

Week 1: choose one customer and one type of job for a pilot. Week 2: enter open jobs into the system and make out the invoices from the details recorded on the job. Week 3: introduce driver sign-offs and POD attachments so the attachments are ready on the job for invoicing. Week 4: invoice the pilot customer electronically and check what is missing before moving everything else across.

The paper CMR still travels with the goods unless an e-CMR is used for the transport; for the first month it is also worth keeping the paper sign-offs as a backup. Finnish Customs and the Finnish Tax Administration may require transport documents during inspections, so check the retention periods directly on the Finnish Tax Administration's website.

A successful switch depends on the driver learning the new way quickly and the customer accepting a digital invoice without resistance. For the driver, go through the mobile sign-off steps before the first job: open the app, select the job, take a photo, ask for a signature, mark as complete. Once learnt, the whole thing takes 30 seconds. For the customer, agree in advance that the invoice will come electronically with a photographed CMR attached rather than a paper one. Most customers accept this because it speeds up their own invoice processing. If a customer insists on a paper invoice, it is worth checking whether this is a real requirement or just habit, since in most cases it is habit rather than a legal requirement.

Where RAHTIS is not (yet) a fit

RAHTIS handles a job from order to archiving in one place, and it is designed to work right down to the owner-driver with a single lorry. But to be honest: RAHTIS is not a full accounting system, so the balance sheet and annual accounts are still handled by your accountant or in accounting software. If you run international loose trailer work through several freight exchanges, ask us directly about integrations with the different platforms before committing.

How do different tools compare for paperless freight invoicing?

The choice depends on whether you need a freight exchange, a transport management system or both in one place. A table from the small haulier's point of view:

An honest weakness: RAHTIS does not replace accounting software and may not cover every exchange job if your customers require a particular system. For hauliers who rely mainly on exchanges, Teleroute or Trans.eu may be the primary place to find work, with invoicing handled on the TMS side.

Your choice of tools also depends on how many different systems you are prepared to use every day. If you find jobs on Trans.eu, run them in Transportial and invoice in Excel, you have three different systems that do not talk to each other. That means every piece of data is moved by hand at least twice, which is exactly the paperwork marathon that going paperless is meant to eliminate. The strength of RAHTIS is that it combines its own offer desk and the TMS in one place, so finding, running and invoicing a job happen in a single chain. This does not mean RAHTIS replaces jobs from other exchanges, but for jobs that come through RAHTIS the documents, invoice status and reminders are all in one place. More information and the application form are at Application · RAHTIS.

FAQ

How much time should paperless invoicing save a small firm?

This guide does not give an exact number of minutes, but the saving comes from data entered once not being copied again from the order to the consignment note and the invoice. When dispatching, invoicing and collecting POD attachments are handled in the same chain, going through and scanning envelopes of receipts in the afternoons disappears altogether, and the invoice can be sent as soon as the goods are delivered.

Is a photographed CMR enough as an invoice attachment?

For most customers it is, but not for all. If the consignee or customer requires the original paper CMR, a digital image only partly replaces it, and the original document must still be kept. The paper CMR travels with the goods in any case unless an e-CMR is used for the transport, so keep the originals, especially during the first month of the switch, and agree the method of sign-off with the customer in advance.

How long must invoices and attachments be kept?

Under the Finnish Accounting Act, vouchers such as invoices and their attachments are kept for at least six years from the end of the year in which the financial year ended, and the financial statements and the books for at least ten years from the end of the financial year. An electronic archive is acceptable as long as the data remains unaltered and accessible throughout. Final responsibility for retention obligations lies with you and your accountant, even if the system handles archiving automatically.

Does RAHTIS replace accounting software?

No. RAHTIS handles a job from order to archiving: the order, consignment note details, driver sign-offs, POD attachments, the invoice status and payment reminders. You make out the invoice in your own invoicing or accounting software, and the balance sheet and annual accounts are still handled by your accountant. So your accountant still needs their own tools, but no longer scraps of paper about jobs.

Do freight exchange jobs fit into the same invoicing process?

Yes. A job taken from an exchange is entered into the system once, with the customer, route and freight rate, and the driver signs off collection and delivery just as for your own customers. Each customer receives its own invoice with its own terms and references, even if the jobs are in the same calendar, and the POD attachment is ready on the job for invoicing.

rr-seuranta-noudosta-toimitukseen.title: Order tracking: the stages of a transport from collection to delivery
rr-seuranta-noudosta-toimitukseen.description: Order tracking shows an order's progress from collection to delivery without GPS units: customers check the status themselves, so fewer calls and notes.
rr-seuranta-noudosta-toimitukseen.html:
Key takeaways

  • Order tracking means following each order stage by stage from collection to delivery, not real-time vehicle location data.
  • Order tracking does not need GPS units, so for a small fleet it is a cheaper and lighter option.
  • Five pieces of information are enough for the customer: status, schedule, exceptions, consignment note number and POD.
  • In loose trailer and container work, the swap is recorded as a separate event so tracking does not break off mid-journey.
  • The biggest problem when introducing it is a status that is not updated, which is solved by making an update a single tap.

Order tracking means following each order as the transport moves through clear statuses: collection, loading, swap, delivery and confirmation of the signed consignment note (POD). This guide shows how to set up the workflow so the customer can see the situation themselves and you save on phone calls, notes and spreadsheets, even if you run loose trailers or swap containers.

What does order tracking mean in practice?

Order tracking means tracking per order: a single consignment is followed step by step from collection to delivery, rather than the lorry's position on a map. In other words, it is about transport events, such as loading, unloading and the consignment note coming back, not vehicle location data.

The distinction matters because many small hauliers currently track only their own lorry or phone the customer to ask about the load. With order tracking, the customer can see what stage their particular job has reached, and the driver marks the stages along the way. Behind the process is the consignment note, which in international transport is the CMR: it is not the contract itself but evidence of the contract of carriage, its terms and the receipt of the goods (Articles 4 and 9 of the CMR Convention), and liability is determined by the Convention.

In practice order tracking can work without a separate GPS system: the driver updates the status, and a system such as RAHTIS (https://www.rahtis.eu/) shows the order's progress all the way to the customer.

How does order tracking differ from real-time vehicle tracking?

Order tracking means status-based tracking: the transport progresses stage by stage from collection to delivery, and the customer can see where their own consignment is. GPS-based vehicle tracking, on the other hand, follows the lorry, not the load. The same lorry may carry three different orders in a day, in which case vehicle tracking tells you where the lorry is, but not whose consignment is on board.

For a small firm, status tracking is often enough, because it tells the customer exactly what they ask on the phone: has the load been collected, is it on its way and has it been delivered. A GPS system adds devices, monthly fees and maintenance, the benefit of which is small for a small fleet.

Order tracking (per order)GPS tracking (per vehicle)
What is trackedAn individual consignmentThe vehicle
Customer visibilityTheir own order, stage by stagePosition of the whole lorry
Needs a deviceNoYes
Best suited toFirms with 1–12 vehiclesLarge fleets

In RAHTIS, order tracking is built straight into the order: you record the stages yourself or the driver marks them, with no separate GPS system. The terms of use describe what the haulier reports to the customer about exceptions, and accurate stage recording also protects you in disputes (https://www.rahtis.eu/en/terms).

When GPS tracking is still needed

GPS tracking is worthwhile if your customer requires real-time lorry location written into the contract, if you run vehicle operating hours or service intervals from the system, or if your fleet is spread across several drivers and you want a fleet manager's view. Theft risk and mandatory monitoring of drivers' working time can also justify a device. In other cases, status tracking meets the customer's needs more cheaply and with less hassle.

What information should you show the customer in order tracking?

The customer needs five things: the current status (collected, in transit, delivered), the estimated schedule, exceptions such as a delay or rerouting, the consignment note number and the POD once the signed delivery note has reached the system. This is enough to eliminate almost every customer service call: when the customer can see the status themselves, they do not ring to ask "where's the lorry?".

Avoid showing the driver's personal details, precise real-time coordinates, freight rates or other customers on the same route. When the vehicle is driven by an identifiable driver, its location data is that driver's personal data, so passing it on is restricted by the EU General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR, Regulation (EU) 2016/679).

In practice you share a link with the customer that shows only that order's details. In RAHTIS this works by the order progressing from collection to delivery and the customer sees the stages with time stamps via a tracking link, without logging in; the API documentation describes how status data can be shared with the customer's own systems (https://www.rahtis.eu/en/api-docs). An honest limitation: RAHTIS does not show a map accurate to the minute – tracking is based on status updates, which is enough for most loose trailer and job-by-job transport.

How are one-off jobs, such as loose trailer and container transport, tracked stage by stage?

Order tracking for loose trailer and container transport is built on four stages: publication, collection, swap and delivery. Each stage is updated as soon as the driver or the transport planner records the event, so the customer can see the situation without phone calls.

Stage 1: publishing and accepting the task

The job is published once, either on the freight exchange or directly to the customer: collection point, destination, vehicle requirement and schedule. Once accepted, the task gets its own reference, around which all later information builds up. A task published in RAHTIS goes straight into your own workflow, so there is no need for separate exchange records or copying into a spreadsheet.

Stage 2: collection and load confirmation

The driver records arrival at the collection point, and loading is confirmed either in the app or with the consignment note details. At this stage it is worth recording the container or trailer number, because it is the only sure way to identify the right unit when the same equipment is used on several jobs. An incorrect container number is the most common reason tracking shows the details of the wrong unit.

Stage 3: swaps and intermediate statuses

In container and loose trailer traffic the load often changes vehicle mid-journey: at a port, a terminal or a partner's yard. The swap is recorded as a separate event, so the time stamps are kept and the customer can see what stage the load is at even when the vehicle changes. Without recording these intermediate stages, tracking breaks off at exactly the points where customers ask most often.

Stage 4: delivery and POD

Delivery is confirmed with a POD: a receipt, signature or photo is attached directly to the task. RAHTIS combines the consignment note, POD and payment tracking for the invoice in the same record: once you mark the invoice on the job, RAHTIS tracks the due date and reminds the customer about an unpaid invoice. Through the API (https://www.rahtis.eu/fi/api-docs) the status can also be passed on to the customer's own system.

How is tracking information shared with the customer automatically?

There are three practical ways: a shared tracking link, email notifications when the status changes and API integration. For most firms with 1–12 vehicles, the first two are enough.

Shared link vs. email notifications

A shared link is the simplest way: once the order is in RAHTIS, you send the customer a link through which they can see the status from collection to delivery. You do not call, the customer does not call you, and you can send the link once and forget about it. Email notifications work when the customer cannot be bothered to click anything: the system sends a message automatically when the status changes, for example "collected" or "delivered".

A shared link has one honest limitation: the customer sees the status only when you update it. If you forget to mark the collection as done, the customer sees out-of-date information. That is why the status is best updated on the phone while on the road, not in a notebook at home in the evening.

API integration

API integration means tracking data goes straight into the customer's own system without emails or links. It is mainly relevant when your customer is large and needs the data in its own system. RAHTIS has an open, free REST API for shippers, with webhooks that report changes in order status (for example order.taken, order.started and order.closed); the documentation is at /api-docs. Even so, an integration is rarely the first step for a small haulier, so it is worth coming back to it when a larger customer asks for it.

Freight exchanges such as Teleroute and Trans.eu are first and foremost places where loads and capacity meet, and their tracking features vary depending on the service and the tools the customer uses. That is why final order tracking and customer communication are best kept in your own systems, not behind an exchange login.

What are the most common tracking problems and how are they solved?

The biggest problem is the driver not updating the status. The solution is to make updating so easy that it needs no call to the transport planner: a single tap on the mobile says that the lorry is at the collection point, loaded or unloaded. When the status is updated from the road, dispatch can see the situation without notes.

The second problem is an exception that goes unreported: a delay, damage or a wrong address. When the order is tracked stage by stage from collection to delivery, the exception is recorded on the same order with a time stamp, so you can tell the customer straight away rather than when they ring.

The third classic is the paper consignment note going missing. The solution is to capture the consignment note and POD digitally the moment delivery is completed and attach them to the order. RAHTIS itself describes how the driver receives the job and status updates directly on their phone and the documents are saved in the system (source).

The fourth problem is the customer ringing with the question "where's the lorry?". When the order status and documents can be shared as a link, you can answer by looking at your own screen. To be honest: if the driver still does not update the status, no system will fix that, so learning the routine is part of getting started.

How do you introduce order tracking as part of transport management?

The first week in practice

Day one: add your own vehicles and drivers to RAHTIS. Day two: take one real job from the freight exchange and run it through the system from collection to POD, without duplicating it on paper. Day three: send the customer the first tracking link and ask whether it looks like what they need. Rest of the week: move the remaining active jobs into the system and deliberately put the notebook aside. If something breaks, fix it in the system rather than going back to the old way.

In a small firm the responsibilities are clear: whoever accepts the job marks its status. The driver updates collection and delivery; you confirm the consignment note and invoicing. One rule is enough: the status changes only in the system, not by agreeing over the phone to do it "later".

Where RAHTIS is enough and where it is not

RAHTIS is enough for what most firms with 1–12 vehicles need order tracking for: the order is tracked stage by stage from collection to delivery, the customer sees the status of their own job without calling, and filling empty legs happens in the same place as dispatch. It does not replace a GPS tracker fitted to the vehicle, so real-time map position and vehicle data come from elsewhere if you want them. Nor is it a full accounting program, although payment tracking for invoices is covered. An honest test: if your customers demand minute-by-minute real-time location or ERP integrations, you need a bigger system alongside it. If what you need is for jobs to progress visibly without phone calls, this is enough.

FAQ

How much does order tracking cost a small haulage firm?

The cost depends on the system, but order-based tracking is typically much cheaper than a GPS solution fitted to the vehicle, because it needs no devices, installation or maintenance. In RAHTIS, tracking is part of the order workflow, so there is no separate tracking charge. When comparing, also count the time saved: fewer calls and notes mean fewer working hours.

Can order tracking be done without a driver app?

Yes, but it shifts the work to the transport planner. Someone has to update the statuses, and if the driver does not do it from their phone, you mark collections, swaps and deliveries yourself based on reports from the road. This works with a small number of jobs, but some of the benefit is lost: statuses lag and the customer's visibility suffers. In practice an app for the driver is the simplest way to keep the information up to date.

Does order tracking also work for one-off jobs taken from a freight exchange?

Yes, and that is where it is most useful. A job taken from a freight exchange gets its own reference, around which collection, load confirmation, any swap and delivery with POD build up. A task published in RAHTIS goes straight into your own workflow without separate records or copying into a spreadsheet. The customer sees the stages of their own consignment even if the same lorry carries several different loads in the course of the day.

How are the POD and consignment note made part of tracking?

The delivery stage is confirmed with a POD: a receipt, signature or photo is attached directly to the order the moment the delivery is completed. That way the paper consignment note does not go missing, and the consignment note, POD and payment tracking for the invoice stay in the same record. Payment reminders go out automatically if an invoice you have marked falls overdue, and the documents can be shared with the customer as a link without chasing email attachments afterwards.

Does order tracking need a separate GPS tracker in the vehicle?

No. Order tracking is based on stage updates recorded by the driver or transport planner along the way, so nothing is fitted to the vehicle. A GPS unit is only worthwhile if your customers require real-time lorry location in the contract, you need maintenance or working time data, or your fleet is so spread out that a fleet manager's view is essential. For most firms with 1–12 vehicles, status information is enough for their customers.

trucking-dispatch-beginners-guide-small-.title: Trucking Dispatch: A Beginner's Guide for Small Carriers
trucking-dispatch-beginners-guide-small-.description: Trucking dispatch explained step by step for 1-12 truck carriers: fill empty trucks, handle CMR and PODs, and decide between a dispatcher, software, or DIY.
trucking-dispatch-beginners-guide-small-.html:
Key takeaways

  • Trucking dispatch is the daily loop of finding loads, confirming rates, assigning drivers, and collecting CMR notes and PODs so you get paid.
  • A hired dispatcher usually takes a percentage of each load's revenue, which can eat most of your margin on thin domestic rates.
  • One person can dispatch 4-12 trucks in roughly one to two hours daily if load boards, dispatch, and invoicing are consolidated in one place.
  • Two fixed check-ins per driver, at loading and delivery, are the practical baseline; other calls should be exception-driven.
  • Free tools and spreadsheets cover job lists but usually stop at rate confirmations, CMR paperwork, POD collection, and invoicing.

Trucking dispatch is the daily work of finding loads on a freight exchange, confirming rates, assigning them to your drivers, checking in on progress, and collecting the CMR notes and PODs so you get paid. This guide walks through one full dispatch day step by step, then helps you decide whether to hire a dispatcher, use software, or keep doing it yourself.

What does a trucking dispatcher actually do day to day?

A dispatcher fills empty trucks, keeps drivers moving, and turns completed jobs into paid invoices. In a 1-12 truck company, that person is often you, doing it between driving, quoting, and chasing paperwork.

The morning: filling empty trucks from the load board

The day starts with the freight exchange or load board: matching trucks that would otherwise run empty (tyhjäajo) against loads that pay well and end somewhere useful for a return load. That means several logins, comparing rates, and booking keikka before drivers finish their morning coffee.

The middle of the day: driver communication and check calls

Once trucks roll, dispatch is answering calls: delays at the terminal, a changed loading time, a detour. Each change means updating the schedule, telling the shipper, and sometimes rebooking a slot. It is reactive work, and it eats the hours you planned for selling.

The end of the day: paperwork, PODs, and who owes what

Evenings go to CMR notes, PODs, and the notebook tracking who owes what. One 4-truck owner described exactly this mess: separate load board logins, an old TMS, and a paper notebook for receivables (Reddit thread). Tools like RAHTIS exist to collapse that loop into one place.

A real dispatch workflow, step by step

Step 1: Search the freight exchange for a return load

Your morning starts with the freight exchange, not your email. You filter by the lane your truck will be empty on, check the weight and trailer type the cargo needs, and shortlist two or three offers worth a call. If you run your own clients, you first check which keikka is already booked, then search the rahtipörssi only for the gap that would otherwise be tyhjäajo. The goal is simple: never let a truck leave a region without a return load confirmed.

Step 2: Quote, agree the price, and get the rate confirmation

You quote based on the lane, the loading windows, and what the customer accepted last time. Once the price is agreed, get it in writing, whether that is a rate confirmation from a broker or an accepted offer on the exchange. A verbal "yes, we'll load you at 14:00" is not a rate confirmation. This document is what your invoice rests on later.

Step 3: Send the job to the driver and set check-in times

Pass the driver the essentials: pickup address, time window, cargo details, contact number, and CMR requirements. Set fixed check-in times, typically at loading and at delivery, so you are not chasing updates by phone all day. Write the check-ins into your dispatch sheet so a missed call is visible within the hour.

Step 4: Handle exceptions: delays, trailer swaps, terminal queues

The plan breaks at the terminal queue, the late shipper, or the trailer that suddenly needs swapping. Your job is to rebook the delivery window, tell the customer before they ask, and log what changed. A dispatcher who documents exceptions calmly is the reason customers come back.

Step 5: Close the job: CMR, POD, invoice, and tracking payment

The job is not done at delivery. You collect the signed CMR and POD, match them to the rate confirmation, invoice, and then track days-to-payment until the money lands. That last stretch, chasing paperwork and unpaid invoices from a paper notebook, is exactly what RAHTIS replaces: publish once, follow the job step by step, and keep CMR, POD, and invoice tied to the same job. If your setup still lives in separate logins and a notebook, that is the loop worth breaking, and you can start by applying at https://www.rahtis.eu/en/apply. Honest caveat: RAHTIS covers dispatch and documents, not accounting, so your bookkeeping stays wherever it is today.

What trucking dispatch terminology do beginners need to know?

Load board, freight exchange, rahtipörssi: same thing, different words

A load board is a marketplace where shippers and forwarders post loads and carriers post available trucks. In Northern Europe the same service is called a freight exchange or rahtipörssi, and the big ones are Teleroute, TIMOCOM and Trans.eu, each requiring its own login (https://www.teleroute.com). Irtoperä means a semitrailer hauled without its own tractor: the shipper or port hands you a loaded trailer and you supply only the tractor and driver. A keikka is a single job.

Rate confirmation, CMR note, POD

TermWhat it isWho issues it
Rate confirmationAgreed price and terms for a loadBroker or shipper
CMR note / rahtikirjaTransport document that travels with the cargo and evidences the contract of carriageSender and carrier; the driver signs for the carrier
PODProof of delivery, signed on arrivalReceiver

Empty running, irtoperä, tyhjäajo, backhaul

Tyhjäajo is a truck driving empty after a drop-off. Dispatchers search the exchange for a return load or backhaul to cover those kilometres; an irtoperä trailer heading your way can be that backhaul, since the tractor going home empty only has to hook it up. RAHTIS (rahtis.eu) puts its own load board, dispatch board and CMR paperwork in one place; it does not pull in loads from other exchanges, so those still need their own logins.

Should a small carrier hire a dispatcher, use dispatch software, or do it themselves?

What hiring a dispatcher costs and when it makes sense

A hired dispatcher is usually paid a percentage of each load's revenue, so on thin Finnish domestic rates that cut can eat most of your margin on irtoperä work. It makes sense when you are sitting in the cab all day and genuinely cannot search the rahtipörssi or answer driver calls. If you are already office-based part of the day, paying someone to do what you could do yourself is hard to justify.

What dispatch software must do for a 1-12 truck fleet

At your size, the software replaces the notebook, not a person. It must handle load searching and booking, driver assignment, CMR paperwork, and tracking who owes what, without per-user pricing that punishes a one-man dispatch office. Tools like Transportial or Trans.eu cover parts of this; a full workflow in one place is what RAHTIS is built for, from published job to paid invoice. Honest limitation: RAHTIS will not negotiate your rates or chase a broker by phone, so you still do the talking.

The honest case for doing it yourself with the right tools

Dispatching your own trucks keeps the margin and builds your customer base directly. The workload is real, roughly an hour or two daily on planning and paperwork, but software that consolidates load boards, dispatch, and invoicing makes that manageable for one person. Start by doing it yourself; hire help only when trucks are sitting idle because you cannot answer the phone.

How does dispatching differ for hotshot trucking versus full-size semi fleets?

Hotshot is the American term for a pickup and gooseneck trailer running smaller, urgent loads. In Finland and Northern Europe the closest equivalent is the van or light truck chasing small part loads and short keikka off the rahtipörssi.

Smaller loads, faster turns

A hotshot dispatcher books more, shorter jobs per day, so the phone work and paperwork multiply even though revenue per load is smaller. Empty running hurts more too: with a light trailer, a return load matters on nearly every trip, not just occasionally. Each international job still needs a CMR note: the UNECE CMR Convention applies to international road carriage for reward regardless of vehicle size, while domestic jobs in Finland run on an ordinary rahtikirja under the Finnish Road Transport Contracts Act (tiekuljetussopimuslaki).

What carries over to any fleet size

The core loop is identical: search the load board, agree the rate, dispatch, track, invoice. RAHTIS handles that loop the same way whether you run one van or twelve semis; on fast-turn freight, expect more calls whatever tool you use.

What does free trucking dispatch software include, and when is it not enough?

What free tiers and spreadsheets actually cover

A spreadsheet or notebook can hold load details, driver names, and who owes what. That is exactly what the 4-truck owner on Reddit described: separate load board logins, an old TMS, and a paper notebook for receivables (Reddit thread). Free tiers of dispatch tools usually add job lists and basic status tracking. That covers the first half of a dispatch day, not the paperwork half.

Where free tools break: per-user pricing, load boards, invoicing

Free tools stop where the money moves. Rate confirmations, CMR notes, POD collection, and invoicing usually sit behind paid plans, and per-user pricing hurts when you are the dispatcher, accountant, and safety guy in one. Load boards also stay separate: you still log into Teleroute, TIMOCOM, or Trans.eu to find irtoperä and backhaul loads, then retype the job into your dispatch sheet.

Running RAHTIS through the same criteria, including its limits

RAHTIS bundles a freight exchange (rahtipörssi) with a TMS, so shippers publish once and carriers fill empty trucks and dispatch in one place, from one truck up. It handles the publish-search-dispatch-invoice loop. Its limits: it will not replace your accounting software, and if your clients load you through other exchanges, those still need their own logins.

How do you train to become a trucking dispatcher without prior experience?

Trucking dispatch classes and courses: what they teach

Paid dispatch courses typically cover load board searching, rate confirmation basics, broker communication, and paperwork like the CMR note. They are useful if you have never touched a freight exchange or a rahtipörssi listing. What they cannot teach is your own lanes, your own drivers, and your own customers, which is where most of the real learning happens anyway.

Learning on your own fleet: a 30-day plan

Week 1: document every job you run, from search to POD, on paper. Week 2: move that paper into one place, replacing the notebook with a spreadsheet or a TMS so who-owes-what stops living in your head. Week 3: standardise check-in times with drivers and file every rate con and rahtikirja the same way. Week 4: review the month, find the slowest step, and fix only that one.

FAQ

How do dispatchers get paid and what does that mean for your margins?

Most hired dispatchers take a percentage of each load's revenue. On thin Finnish domestic rates, especially irtoperä work, that cut can consume most of your margin. If you are office-based part of the day, paying someone to search the rahtipörssi and answer driver calls is hard to justify; hire help only when trucks sit idle because you cannot answer the phone.

Can one person realistically dispatch 4-12 trucks while doing accounting and safety?

Yes, with the right tools. Dispatching your own fleet takes roughly an hour or two daily on planning and paperwork, and software that consolidates load boards, dispatch, and invoicing makes that manageable for one person. The realistic limit is phone time: one person can plan the day, but exceptions at terminals are what stretch the hours.

Do I need a trucking dispatch course before dispatching my own trucks?

Not necessarily. Paid courses teach load board searching, rate confirmations, and paperwork like the CMR note, which helps if you have never touched a freight exchange. They cannot teach your own lanes, drivers, and customers. A 30-day plan on your own fleet, documenting every job from search to POD, covers most of the real learning.

What is the difference between a freight exchange and a TMS?

A freight exchange, or rahtipörssi, is a marketplace where shippers post loads and carriers post available trucks; Teleroute, TIMOCOM, and Trans.eu are examples. A TMS is your internal system for running jobs: driver assignment, CMR paperwork, and tracking who owes what. Most small carriers juggle both separately; some tools now bundle them in one place.

How many check calls should a dispatcher make per driver per day?

Two fixed check-ins per driver is the practical baseline: one at loading and one at delivery. Write them into your dispatch sheet so a missed call is visible within the hour. Beyond that, calls should be exception-driven, triggered by delays, terminal queues, or trailer swaps, rather than chasing updates by phone all day.

tyhjan-peravaunun-kontin-palautusreitin-.title: Planning the return route for an empty trailer or container
tyhjan-peravaunun-kontin-palautusreitin-.description: Planning the return route for an empty trailer or container: work out the cost of running empty, set a floor price for a backload and track empty running monthly.
tyhjan-peravaunun-kontin-palautusreitin-.html:
Key takeaways

  • Work out the cost of running empty per kilometre and set a floor price: a backload paying less than that is not worth taking.
  • Look for a backload before the lorry sets off, not once it is standing empty at the delivery point.
  • The container return deadline, the container depot's opening hours and the driver's remaining driving time constrain the route before you commit to it.
  • Track three figures for each vehicle every month: empty running percentage, cost per empty kilometre and how many return legs were run loaded.
  • Freight exchanges such as Trans.eu and TIMOCOM are sources of backloads; RAHTIS shows loads near the delivery point from its own load board, but does not pull offers from other exchanges.

Planning the return route for an empty trailer or container starts with euros: work out the cost of running empty (fuel, tyres, maintenance, driver time) and compare it with the rate for a backload, minus the cost of any detour and waiting time. This guide gives you a decision model for when to take a backload and when to run empty, plus a checklist for planning the route.

Why does returning an empty trailer or container cost money?

Running empty costs almost as much as running loaded: you burn slightly less fuel, but the driver is still being paid and the vehicle wears just the same. There is simply no revenue. According to Statistics Finland's road freight statistics, in the 2010s around a quarter (23–29 %) of lorry kilometres were driven empty, and that shows up directly in the margin.

Which costs arise even when the lorry is empty

Fuel, driver wages, insurance, tyres, servicing and depreciation all accrue when the lorry is empty too. On top of that there is the opportunity cost: every hour a trailer stands empty waiting to be returned is an hour you could have used for a paid job. The freight revenue disappears; the costs do not.

Why empty running builds up unnoticed in a small firm

When you handle dispatch, invoicing and safety yourself, looking for a backload easily ends up at the bottom of the list. Empty running does not appear on any invoice; it just vanishes into the margin. That is why the first step is to record every empty kilometre, for example in a system such as RAHTIS, where jobs and vehicles are in the same view.

When is a backload worth taking, and when is it not?

The decision is made in euros, not on gut feeling: if the backload rate covers the variable costs and part of the fixed costs, take it. If not, running empty may be the more sensible choice.

The floor price in euros: how to calculate the lowest acceptable rate

First work out the cost of running empty: kilometres × variable cost per kilometre (diesel, tyres, mileage-related maintenance) + driver time. The floor price is that total plus a small margin, say 5–10 %. A backload below the floor does not even cover the cost of the return leg itself, and it takes up time you could spend on a better-paying job.

Three situations where an empty return is the right choice

  1. The backload rate is below the floor and negotiation will not lift it above.
  2. Loading or unloading the backload would delay your own job the next day, which has a better margin.
  3. The container or trailer has its own return deadline, and collecting the load would push the return past it.

Worked example: a 400 km return leg to southern Finland

ItemAmount
Diesel, 400 km × 30 l/100 km × €1.75/l (example price)€210
Driver time, 5 h × €25€125
Other variable costs (tyres, maintenance)€60
Total cost of running empty€395
Floor price (+10 %)approx. €435

If a freight exchange such as Trans.eu or TIMOCOM has a backload on the same lane for more than €435 and it does not require a detour, take it. A load below that costs you money. Run the numbers with your own vehicle's fuel consumption and your own wage costs, as the figures in the example are only indicative.

How do you plan the return route step by step?

Steps 1–3: the basics before the lorry sets off

Step 1: record where and when the lorry will be empty. Step 2: work out the cost per kilometre of running empty. Fuel and driver wages are the largest cost items in road haulage, so estimate them realistically. Step 3: look for a backload before departure, not once the lorry is standing empty at the delivery point.

Steps 4–5: choosing the backload and fitting the schedule

Step 4: compare backloads on two measures: the rate and the deviation from your route. A load that pays less but heads straight towards home often beats one that pays more but takes the lorry 200 km in the wrong direction. Step 5: fit the loading and unloading times so that they do not put the original job at risk. If the backload's loading slot forces the driver to wait until the next day, the overnight stop eats up the earnings.

Steps 6–7: fixing the route and briefing the driver

Step 6: lock in the route and update the schedule in both directions, so that another job for the customer does not derail the return. Step 7: give the driver clear instructions in a language they understand: loading point, times, how delivery is to be confirmed and whom to call if anything changes.

At this stage a paper notebook is no longer enough. When the job, the consignment note and the invoice are in the same system, nothing has to be copied a second time. In RAHTIS, the job, the driver's sign-off and the invoice to your own customer are in one place, and while the lorry is still on the road you can see loads near the delivery point on the RAHTIS load board. You can set a load alert on saved routes to be notified of suitable new loads.

Which factors affect the choice of return route (distance, timing, container availability)?

The choice of route depends on distance, timing, where the container or trailer is to be returned, the opening hours of the port or container depot, the driver's remaining driving time, fuel costs and the going rate for backloads. Always check the return location, opening hours and driving time before you promise the customer a return.

Port and container depot return times

Empty container returns often fail because the depot or terminal is closed by the time the lorry arrives. Check the opening hours in advance and note them with the route. If the last return time is 16:00 and loading runs late, the return slips to the next day and the lorry stands idle overnight.

Return location and deadline

The return location for an empty container is usually set by the shipping line or its agent, and there is a period of free time for the return, after which detention or demurrage charges start to accrue. Check the return reference, the return location and the last return date before you lock in the route. If you only have one day, picking up a backload on the same route is effectively ruled out and the empty run is already decided.

The driver's driving and rest times

The return route has to be calculated from the driver's remaining driving time, not the distance on the map. If the driver has four hours of driving time left and the return would take six, the route will not fit into the day and the overnight stop eats up the backload revenue. Check the remaining driving time from the tachograph or the driver card data before confirming the route, and record the return on the job so that the driver sees the same schedule as you do.

Fuel price and detours

The price of diesel varies by region and by week, which directly affects whether the detour a backload requires is worth making. If a backload requires an 80 km detour and diesel costs €1.85 a litre, the fuel alone comes to about €44 at a consumption of 30 l/100 km. Add driver time and tyre wear, and the detour easily costs €60–70 or more. If the backload does not bring in more than that, running home empty is cheaper. Update your calculations monthly so that the floor price stays realistic.

How do backloads and freight exchanges help reduce empty running?

On a freight exchange you search for loads that fit your route and timing, and you see who is willing to pay so that your lorry does not run home empty. Exchanges used in the Nordic countries include TIMOCOM, Teleroute and Trans.eu. The principle is the same: you see the offers and the shipper's details before you commit.

Search by route, not by a single town

Do not just look for loads "from Turku"; look along a route that matches your direction. Search by origin and destination region and allow a reasonable detour, say 50–100 km. Remember that driving and rest times limit how long a detour you can make without the return slipping to the next day (Regulation (EC) No 561/2006). Always do the maths: the backload rate minus the fuel and time for the detour, compared with running straight home empty.

Several exchanges side by side

On secondary routes in the Nordic countries, a single exchange has thin coverage, so many small hauliers follow two or three exchanges in parallel. The same load and the same shipper may then appear in several places, and the details are copied by hand into your own system. RAHTIS does not aggregate offers from other exchanges: it shows the loads on its own load board and your own customers' jobs, and you record a job obtained elsewhere yourself.

Checking the shipper's background and payment terms

Before committing to a backload, check out the shipper. The large exchanges usually show a company profile and ratings from other users; also check the business ID (Y-tunnus, the Finnish company registration number) and company details, for example in the Finnish Business Information System YTJ, and, if the relationship continues, the reports required under the Finnish Contractor's Liability Act. If the ratings are poor or the payment period is long, you may end up waiting for your money.

In that case, either agree a shorter payment period in writing or choose another load, even if the rate is slightly lower. For a small firm, a single late invoice can wipe out the entire margin on the backload.

How does software help you manage empty returns?

What to demand from a transport management system for a small firm

When you handle dispatch, invoicing and safety yourself, the job of software is to reduce scraps of paper and separate logins, not add to them. Demand the following: backloads appear in the same view as your own jobs, vehicles and drivers are entered once, the driver's sign-off and the consignment note are linked to the invoice, and you can see who has paid and who has not. Container haulage also needs visibility of return times and deadlines, because return times and detention charges vary by shipping line and by depot.

RAHTIS against the same criteria

In RAHTIS, vehicles, trailers and drivers are entered once, the driver signs off the job in the app (signature, photos and consignment note), and you can invoice your own customer for the job from the same place and track whether the invoice has been paid. You can see backloads near the delivery point on the RAHTIS load board. Freight exchanges such as Trans.eu or TIMOCOM remain separate services, and RAHTIS does not replace them. Pricing is per vehicle: the first vehicle is free and each additional vehicle that has run jobs costs €14.90 a month (excl. VAT).

How do you track and reduce empty running month by month?

Three figures to calculate every month

The first figure is the empty running percentage: empty kilometres divided by all kilometres driven. Calculate it separately for each vehicle, so you can see which route is eating into your margin.

The second figure is the cost per empty kilometre. Take the vehicle's monthly cost (fuel, driver, insurance, depreciation) and divide it by all kilometres driven: an empty kilometre costs in practice the same as a loaded one. Once you know that a kilometre costs, say, €1.20, accepting or rejecting a backload becomes a simple calculation.

The third figure is the load factor on return legs: how many return legs were run loaded.

Once a month, pick three actions: go through the routes of your worst-performing vehicle, ask two regular customers for backloads in advance and check the exchange offers before the lorry becomes free. Record the figures in the same spreadsheet as your unpaid invoices.

Monthly report and spotting trends

Once you have three months of figures, compare them. If the empty running percentage rises from month to month, a route or customer is causing recurring empty running. Find it and either negotiate a fixed-price backload or drop the route. Record every action in the same spreadsheet, so that three months later you can see whether the fix worked. A small firm has no time for heavy analysis, but a ten-minute check is enough to see which way the figures are moving.

FAQ

How much does an empty kilometre cost in Finland?

There is no general figure. Take the vehicle's monthly cost, i.e. fuel, driver wages including employer contributions, insurance, tyres, servicing and depreciation, and divide it by the kilometres driven in the month. The example in this article used €1.20 per kilometre. The figure varies by vehicle and type of operation, so calculate it separately for each vehicle.

Can a container be returned to a different place from where it was collected?

Sometimes, but it has to be agreed in advance with the shipping line or its agent. Ask for the return reference, the permitted return location and the last return date at the same time. Different depots have different opening hours and charging practices, so another return location may make the route work or shift the return by a day. Check the opening hours before you lock in the route.

Should I take a cheap backload or run empty?

Work out the floor price: the cost of running empty plus a small margin, say 5–10 per cent. If the backload rate is below that and negotiation will not lift it, running empty is the right choice. The same applies if loading or unloading would delay a better job the next day, or if the container return deadline would be missed.

How do I find a backload quickly when the lorry is already empty?

Search the freight exchange by origin and destination region, not just by town, and allow a 50–100 km detour. Compare loads on two measures: the rate and the deviation from your route. Deduct the fuel and time for the detour from the rate, and check the driver's remaining driving time so that the return does not slip to the next day.

Can the driver look for a backload on their phone?

Technically yes, as the exchanges run in a browser, but the driver cannot and must not compare offers while driving. A better model is for you to find the load and give the driver clear instructions: loading point, times, how delivery is to be confirmed and a contact for when plans change. When the route and schedule are agreed in advance, there are fewer phone calls.

tyhjien-ajokilometrien-vahentaminen-pien.title: Reducing empty kilometres with a small vehicle
tyhjien-ajokilometrien-vahentaminen-pien.description: Reducing empty kilometres with a small van: find a backload before unloading, plan the day as a round trip and track your empty running.
tyhjien-ajokilometrien-vahentaminen-pien.html:
Key takeaways

  • Look for a backload before unloading, not once the vehicle is standing empty.
  • Plan the day as a round trip, not as a string of one-off transports, so there is a load for the return leg.
  • With a small vehicle, the margin per job is small, so a few dozen empty kilometres a day can eat up a significant share of the day's margin.
  • Track the share of empty running weekly: empty kilometres divided by all kilometres driven.
  • Regular customers' rounds as the backbone, with freight exchange loads to fill the gaps, produce less empty running than one-off loads picked up here and there.

Reducing empty kilometres with a small vehicle comes down to three things: look for a backload before unloading, combine jobs and customer routes on the same day, and track the share of empty running every week. With a vehicle under 3.5 tonnes, an empty kilometre weighs relatively more than with heavy equipment, because the margin per transport is lower. This guide focuses on van and light goods vehicle work, not on planning heavy combination traffic.

Why do empty kilometres eat a bigger share of the margin with a small vehicle?

In light haulage, empty running is financially more critical than in heavy haulage, because the load, and with it the freight rate, is small, while the vehicle's costs keep running. When a van runs empty, revenue is zero, but fuel, wear and driver time cost almost as much as when it is loaded.

Cost structure: fixed and variable costs for a vehicle under 3.5 tonnes

Fixed costs, such as insurance, vehicle tax, depreciation and lease payments, run every day, whether the vehicle is driven or not. Among variable costs, fuel and driver time weigh heavily with light vehicles, because the margin per hour is small. One empty hour therefore takes a large share of the day's margin. With a heavy combination, an empty kilometre is more expensive, but freight rates are higher and the cost is spread over more tonnes.

Worked example: what an empty day means over a month

If a light vehicle works 22 days a month and one day is spent entirely empty, about 4–5 per cent of working days earn nothing. Two empty days push the share to about nine per cent. Empty running is significant in heavy haulage too: according to Statistics Finland, 23 per cent of the kilometres driven by Finnish-registered lorries were driven empty in 2016 (Statistics Finland, road freight transport). No equivalent statistics are published for vans, so your own tracking is the only reliable figure. Every backload you find goes straight to the margin.

Where can backloads be found for light vehicles?

Backloads for a van can be found in three places: freight exchanges, your own customers and direct cooperation with other hauliers. The largest exchanges, such as TIMOCOM, Teleroute and Trans.eu, mainly serve heavy vehicles, so search for light vehicle loads using filters rather than browsing.

Assessing a freight exchange from a light vehicle perspective

Compare exchanges with three questions: how many loads under 3.5 tonnes appear on your route each week, does the search work by weight, vehicle type and timing, and can you agree terms directly with the shipper through the posting?

CriterionWhat to check
Number of light vehicle loadsFilter for your own route and count the hits over a week
Search and alertsDoes filtering work by weight, vehicle type and timing?
Contact with the shipperBy phone or message, and how quickly do replies come?

RAHTIS has its own load board, where shippers post transports. The backload view shows load board loads near your vehicle's delivery point, and a load alert notifies you when a suitable transport appears on a saved route. RAHTIS does not gather loads from other exchanges into the same view. Load availability varies by region on every exchange, so test your own route before committing.

Be findable: have your posting and alerts ready

A backload is often found because the shipper knows your vehicle is free. Keep a vehicle posting ready on the exchange, showing the vehicle, capacity, time available and return area. Set route alerts before you set off, not once you are already driving empty.

How do you plan routes and runs to leave less empty running?

The day's round trip before the single transport

Plan the day as a round trip, not as a string of one-off transports. When you look at the day as a whole first thing in the morning, you can see straight away which run has an empty return and where you should look for a backload.

A light vehicle's cost structure turns this into real money: fuel and wear make up a large part of the cost per kilometre, so an empty kilometre costs almost as much as a loaded one. Because the margin per job is small, a few dozen empty kilometres a day can take a significant share of the day's margin. Work out your own figure: multiply the empty kilometres by your own cost per kilometre and compare the total with the day's margin.

A practical routine: in the morning, write down the starting point, the delivery points and the estimated time the vehicle will be free. Then check whether there is a load in the return direction that fits the schedule and the size of the vehicle. If not, widen the round: a second customer in the same direction may fill the return leg. In RAHTIS, your own jobs, dispatch and backloads from the load board are in the same service, so checking is quicker than jumping between different services. The system does not plan the route for you, however; it makes the round visible.

Early information saves the backload

A backload is often agreed hours before unloading. If you only hear about a load when the vehicle is already leaving empty, the opportunity has gone. Agree with your customers that you will get load details in good time, and allow a 30–60 minute buffer in the day between unloading and the next loading.

What role do local and regional rounds play?

Regular customers as the backbone, the freight exchange to fill the gaps

Regular customers fill the kilometres you cannot get from a freight exchange. When you have a weekly round with a factory, a distribution point or a construction site, you know the start and end points in advance. That makes looking for a backload realistic: you search the exchange for a load that fits your round's route and schedule.

In practice, this works best when fixed rounds cover the core kilometres and exchange loads fill the gaps. When jobs, proof of delivery and invoices are in the same system, the invoice for a regular round customer does not get forgotten in a paper notebook in between exchange loads (RAHTIS).

A familiar area beats nationwide coverage

When you drive in the same area, you know where unloading happens in the afternoons and who has loads on Mondays. Local knowledge cuts empty kilometres more than any tool: you learn customers' unloading times, the congestion and the yards where a phone call will get you a backload.

Nationwide coverage sounds safer, but with a small vehicle it often means driving to unfamiliar places with no return load. Two or three familiar areas where rounds and exchange loads overlap produce less empty running than one-off loads to different parts of Finland.

How do a freight exchange and a transport management system together reduce empty running?

A freight exchange tells you where loads are. A management system tells you where your own vehicles are and when they become free. When both are visible at the same time, the search for a backload starts from the route: you look at where the vehicle has to go anyway, and find a load going there.

One place for your own jobs and the load board

Many small hauliers have separate exchange logins, Excel and paper notes. In RAHTIS, your own customers' jobs, dispatch, load board transports, consignment notes and invoices are in the same service. For each transport, the load board also shows an estimate of how many kilometres your vehicle would drive empty to the collection point. Hauliers can apply at rahtis.eu/en/apply.

RAHTIS, honestly: where it helps and where it doesn't

RAHTIS does not guarantee loads and does not aggregate loads from other exchanges. It shortens the path from quote to invoice and shows backloads from its own load board, but you find loads and rates from other exchanges in their own services.

Alternatives: TIMOCOM, Teleroute and Trans.eu

TIMOCOM, Teleroute and Trans.eu are each separate freight exchanges, and their light vehicle offering and prices should be checked directly with each service. If you use several exchanges in parallel, work out how much time the separate logins take, and focus on the one that actually has loads for your route.

What mistakes do small-vehicle operators most often make in load planning?

Looking for a backload only once the vehicle is already empty

The most common mistake is looking for a backload only once the delivery has been made and the vehicle is standing idle. By then you have minutes, and the options are to take any load at all or drive home empty. A better way is to look for a backload before you commit to the outbound transport. If no return load is in sight, price the outbound transport to cover both directions.

The second pitfall is keeping the books in a paper notebook: when the information about who owes what lives in your head, the share of empty running is not visible anywhere and you cannot fix it.

Too wide a search area and poor pricing

Many search for loads across the whole country and drive 150 kilometres empty to chase a "cheap" job. With a light vehicle, the freight rate also has to cover the empty run to collection and the empty return, or the kilometres eat the margin.

To be honest: RAHTIS does not automatically calculate the margin per route or the share of empty running. The profitability view shows each vehicle's job revenue and costs, but you track empty kilometres yourself. The first vehicle is free, and each additional vehicle that has run jobs costs €14.90 a month (excl. VAT).

How do you track the share of empty running in practice?

A simple measure: empty kilometres / all kilometres

The measure is a single division: kilometres driven empty divided by all kilometres driven. At the end of each day, write down how many kilometres you drove loaded and how many empty. Paper or a spreadsheet is fine, as long as you record it every day.

If the empty share is over a third, more than one kilometre in three is driven without revenue. The figure tells you whether to look harder for backloads or to price the empty return into the outbound job.

Monthly review and what to do with the figures

Once a month, look at three figures: the share of empty running, the route or customer that caused the most empty running, and the load you missed out on. With one vehicle, 50 empty kilometres a day over 22 working days a month comes to about 1,100 kilometres for which you pay fuel and wear with no revenue.

Use the figures to make decisions: if a particular customer consistently leaves you with an empty return, build it into the rate or drop the customer. The measure does not replace planning, but it shows you where planning should start.

FAQ

How high a share of empty running is still profitable with a small vehicle?

There is no universal limit, because it depends on freight rates and your own costs. As a point of comparison: according to Statistics Finland, 23 per cent of lorry kilometres were driven empty in 2016. If your own share is well over a third, more than one kilometre in three earns nothing, and you should look at how you find backloads or how you price. Track the share weekly and make decisions based on the monthly review.

Are there loads on freight exchanges for vehicles under 3.5 tonnes?

Yes, although the largest exchanges, such as TIMOCOM, Teleroute and Trans.eu, mainly serve heavy vehicles. Search using filters for weight, vehicle type and timing. Load availability varies by region, so first count how many suitable loads appear on your route each week before committing to one exchange.

How do I price the outbound transport if no backload can be found?

If no return load is found before you commit, price the outbound transport to cover both directions. With a light vehicle, the margin per job is small, so an empty return can take a large share of the day's margin. If a particular customer consistently leaves you with an empty return, build it into the rate or drop the customer.

Do I need separate routing software, or is a map app enough?

A map app is enough for driving, but it does not show your jobs, available loads or the share of empty running. What matters is not routing but seeing your own jobs and the available loads in good time. Without that, you look for a backload too late.

tyotuntien-vahentaminen-kitka-auditointi.title: Cutting working hours: a friction audit for small haulage firms
