tyotuntien-vahentaminen-kitka-auditointi.description: Cut working hours with a friction audit: list, measure and remove unnecessary admin. Same volume of haulage, fewer hours in the office.
tyotuntien-vahentaminen-kitka-auditointi.html:
Key takeaways

  • Cutting working hours here means cutting unnecessary admin, not driving fewer kilometres or laying people off.
  • A one-week log, recording how many times and how many minutes each recurring task takes, reveals the biggest sources of friction.
  • A score of frequency × duration × risk of error tells you which source of friction to tackle first.
  • The order: duplicated work first, then manual data transfer, and reporting last.
  • One measure is enough for tracking: admin hours per week, recorded once a month.

You cut working hours by removing friction: unnecessary admin, overlapping tools and hand-compiled reports that eat up your evenings without a single lorry running any more. This guide gives you a step-by-step, measurable friction audit for listing, measuring and prioritising the sources of friction. The result: fewer hours in the office, the same or greater volume on the road.

What does cutting working hours mean in practice in a small firm?

Cutting working hours here does not mean redundancies or driving fewer kilometres. It means cutting your own admin: scraps of paper, separate invoicing and dispatch programs, and evenings spent working out who has paid and who has not.

Why cutting working hours does not mean fewer jobs

A haulage firm's output is the jobs it runs, and those should be left alone. What should be cut is everything else: searching for loads on different exchanges, collecting signed delivery notes, putting invoices together and remembering which invoices are unpaid. Many owner-operators work long weeks, and much of that time goes on things other than the actual business.

When one tool handles the job, the driver's sign-off and the invoice in a single chain, hours are saved without a single lorry being left in the yard. If you are considering this for your own firm, you can apply for a RAHTIS trial here: Apply · RAHTIS.

How does reducing friction cut working hours?

Friction or real work: a definition

Friction is recurring work that takes time but generates neither freight revenue nor customer relationships. Raising invoices by hand, matching signed delivery notes and transport orders to attach to the invoice, separate logins for every freight exchange and a notebook in which you track who owes whom are all friction. Real work is dispatch decisions, negotiating with customers and keeping the lorries on schedule. The rule is simple: if a task repeats on every load and requires no judgement, it can be handed over to a tool. In RAHTIS, the driver signs off the delivery in the app, an invoice to your own customer is created from the job, and a reminder is sent for an unpaid invoice.

Why friction grows as the firm grows

A one-lorry firm can get by on memory and email, because there are few jobs. With five or twelve lorries, every job multiplies the same admin: more invoices, more exchange searches and more outstanding receivables. Admin grows with the number of jobs, but there are still only so many hours in a day. That is why removing friction is the best way to cut working hours without reducing the volume of haulage.

How do I identify the biggest sources of friction?

A friction audit starts with one week and one notebook. Record every recurring admin task: calls to drivers, searching exchanges for loads, invoicing, collecting signed delivery notes, checking hours and rest periods. No estimates, just the actual minutes.

Step 1: Log a week's admin tasks

Keep your phone or a sheet of paper within reach all week. Note each task as soon as you do it, not from memory in the evening. By the end of the week you will have a list that surprises you: many people find tasks they had never thought of as "work" at all.

Step 2: Note frequency and duration

Two figures for each line: how many times a week, and how many minutes each time. Multiply them together to get the task's weekly hours. This is the figure you will compare later when choosing tools.

TaskTimes/weekMin/timeTotal/week
Searching exchanges for loads1582 h
Invoicing and signed delivery notes5252 h 5 min
"Where's the lorry?" calls2051 h 40 min

Step 3: Separate friction from valuable work

Customer work, negotiating rates and safety matters are valuable work. Copying data from one system to another, entering the same load in three places and working out "who has paid" are friction. Do not count drivers' rest periods as friction: the EU driving and rest time regulation (Regulation (EC) No 561/2006) requires them, and monitoring them is statutory work, not unnecessary admin. Once the list is complete, the job of a tool is to remove entirely the lines that are nothing but copying.

In what order should you cut working hours?

Scoring: frequency, duration, risk of error

Score each task found in the audit on three scales: how often it recurs (daily = 3, weekly = 2, monthly = 1), how long it takes each time (over 30 min = 3, 10–30 min = 2, under 10 min = 1) and how easily mistakes happen (an amount to be invoiced or a sign-off = 3, data transfer = 2, a to-do list = 1). Multiply the figures together. The highest score tells you where to start.

An example: the "who has paid" notebook recurs daily (3), often takes over half an hour (3) and a mistake costs money directly (3), so it scores 27. A monthly transport report that takes a quarter of an hour and where a mistake is harmless scores 1 × 2 × 1 = 2. The order is clear.

The order: duplicated work first, then manual transfer, reporting last

Fix duplicated work first, because it removes two tasks at once: when the job details, your own vehicle and the invoice are in one place, you no longer copy the same transport order into two systems. This is the point at which many small haulage firms find that consolidating tools pays for itself fastest: separate exchange logins, an old program and a notebook are replaced by a workflow in which the job is entered once, the driver signs off the delivery, the invoice goes out and payment is tracked. In RAHTIS, this chain runs from job to invoice; jobs come from your own customers and the RAHTIS load board, but it does not bring in loads from other freight exchanges. It is worth reading the terms of use before committing to any system. Second, make manual data transfer, such as recording drivers' hours or refuelling, electronic. Reporting comes last, because it is done least often and is the easiest to replace with a ready-made report or export.

Which tools remove the most friction for a small haulage firm?

Separate freight exchanges or an integrated system

In most small firms, friction comes from three places: separate exchange logins, a separate transport management program or Excel, and a scrap of paper recording who has paid. TIMOCOM, Teleroute and Trans.eu take care of finding loads, but invoicing and signed delivery notes remain separate jobs, and you glue the systems together in the evenings.

An integrated system means that the same tool shows the jobs, records the runs, stores the driver's sign-off and generates the invoice. When the transport order, sign-off and invoice are in the same chain, the "who still owes us" folder disappears, and you no longer have to copy data from one program to another in the evenings.

RAHTIS against the same criteria

RAHTIS brings together in one service your fleet and drivers, your own customers and jobs, the load board and invoicing of your own customers, and the driver signs off the delivery in the app. The API is described in the RAHTIS API documentation. Price: the first vehicle is free, and each additional vehicle that has run jobs during the month costs €14.90 a month (excl. VAT); the first month is free, and no percentage is charged on jobs. RAHTIS is not a large pan-European marketplace like the freight exchanges, but an everyday tool for a small haulage firm, so you can keep using the exchanges to find loads.

How does cutting working hours affect volume and quality?

Removing friction does not reduce the number of jobs. You have just as many lorries, but the time spent on admin is freed up for other things: sales, customer service or rest. When invoices and signed delivery notes are compiled in one place, errors decrease and invoices reach the customer sooner, which speeds up payment.

What to use the freed-up hours for

Decide in advance where the freed-up hours will go. Three realistic options for a small haulage firm:

  1. Sales and customers. Call one more customer a week, or reprice your regular customers' fixed routes.
  2. Backloads. Actively look for backloads, so empty running falls and every kilometre earns more.
  3. Rest. An overloaded owner makes mistakes in dispatch and invoicing. Staying fresh is a quality factor in itself.

Quality improves from the customer's point of view too: when the status of jobs and payments is clear without paper notes, the phone rings less often and answers come faster. Fewer hours are spent, but delivery reliability and invoicing accuracy improve.

How do you track the hours saved without adding more admin?

One measure is enough

Once a month, record a single figure: admin hours per week. Compare it with the level measured before the changes. If the figure falls and the volume of haulage has not dropped, the change worked. If you have no baseline, estimate it in the first month, even roughly.

The same principle works when comparing tools. When you compare freight exchanges such as TIMOCOM, Trans.eu or Teleroute, the measure is the same: how many minutes it takes to find and record one load, and how many empty kilometres were left over each week.

Do not build reporting around the tracking. If collecting the measure takes more than five minutes a month, it is a new source of friction, not a solution.

Which mistakes slow down cutting working hours?

Too many changes at once

The most common mistake is trying to fix everything at once. If you change your invoicing program, freight exchange and dispatch routines in the same month, you will not know what worked and what did not. Pick one source of friction, such as the "who has paid" notebook, and sort it out before moving on to the next.

The second pitfall is overlapping tools. Separate exchange logins, an old program and a scrap of paper do the same work three times over. Consolidating tools only cuts hours if you drop the old way of working at the same time.

Mistaking breaks and rest for friction

The third mistake is cutting in the wrong place. Meal breaks, enough sleep and drivers' rest periods are not friction but a precondition for safe, good-quality work. Drivers' breaks and rest periods are statutory obligations and are not up for negotiation.

Forgetting to measure is the fourth stumbling block. If you do not record the hours for weeks 1–4, you will not see whether the time spent on invoicing went down or simply moved somewhere else.

FAQ

How many hours can a small haulage firm realistically save?

That depends on the starting point, which is why the one-week log is essential. In the example table, three tasks took almost six hours a week just for exchange searches, invoicing and calls. Add the other recurring routines, and admin can come to around ten hours a week, part of which is copying that can be eliminated.

Should a small firm adopt a transport management system or keep doing things by hand?

The deciding question is whether the tool removes lines from your audit list. Maintaining an old program and separate exchanges can itself be friction if the data still have to be combined by hand in the evenings. A system pays for itself fastest when the job is entered once and invoicing, signed delivery notes and payment tracking follow from the same chain.

How do I start the audit if I don't even have time for that?

Start smaller than you think: keep your phone in your pocket and note each task as soon as you do it. A note takes seconds, not a separate work session. If even that seems impossible, measure one day and multiply the figures by five. A rough baseline is enough for comparison.

Does RAHTIS charge for every registered vehicle or only those that have run jobs?

Only those that have run jobs. The first vehicle is free, and each additional vehicle that has run jobs during the month costs €14.90 a month (excl. VAT); an idle vehicle costs nothing. The first month is free, so you can try the system during the audit and compare the hours freed up with your own weekly list.

Will revenue fall if working hours are cut?

Not in this model, because the kilometres driven are not reduced. The time cut is admin that generated no freight revenue. The freed-up hours can go on sales, finding backloads or rest, so the volume of haulage stays the same or grows, invoicing errors decrease and payments come in faster.

vahinkokuvien-liittaminen-toimitukseen-k.title: Attaching damage photos to a delivery from the driver
vahinkokuvien-liittaminen-toimitukseen-k.description: Damage photos in the RAHTIS driver app: photos are saved on the job with time and location, and are sent from the queue once the connection returns.
vahinkokuvien-liittaminen-toimitukseen-k.html:
Key takeaways

  • Damage photos are taken during the inspection at the delivery point, before the consignee signs and before the stop is marked as done.
  • Photos are taken with the app's own Take photo button, so they are saved directly to the right job and stop, and the location is recorded at the moment the button is pressed.
  • A good basic set is an overall shot of the damaged side, a close-up of the damage and a shot showing the trailer, container or seal number.
  • A weak signal does not stop you taking photos: the app holds them in a queue and sends them in order when the connection returns.
  • A photo does not replace a note on the consignment note: in CMR carriage, apparent damage must be noted no later than at delivery, and in other cases written reservations must be made within seven days.

The driver attaches damage photos to a delivery in the RAHTIS driver app by opening the job, pressing Arrived at the delivery point, photographing the damaged area during the inspection and marking it as new damage before the stop is marked as done. This guide covers the steps, photo quality and what to do when the signal is weak at a port or terminal.

When must damage photos be attached to the delivery?

Damage photos are taken at the delivery point before or during unloading, before the consignee signs and at the latest before the stop is marked as done. When the photo is saved to the same job straight away, it shows what condition the goods and equipment were in at the moment of delivery, and nobody has to guess whether the damage happened only after unloading in the consignee's warehouse.

Timing also matters because of the time limits. Under section 40 of the Finnish Road Transport Contracts Act (345/1979), which for international carriage corresponds to Article 30 of the CMR Convention, the consignee must make reservations about apparent damage no later than at the time of delivery, and about other damage in writing within seven days, excluding Sundays and public holidays. In international carriage, the absence of reservations means that the goods are deemed to have been delivered in the condition described in the consignment note, unless proven otherwise. In domestic carriage, failing to make reservations generally means losing the right to bring a claim (Road Transport Contracts Act, Finlex). A photo timestamped at the moment of delivery is stronger evidence than one sent a couple of days later.

A practical rule of thumb for drivers: take the photos during unloading, record the damage in the app and on the consignment note straight away, and only then take the consignee's signature. That way the signed proof of delivery and the damage photos are on the same job.

How does the driver attach damage photos to the delivery, step by step?

The driver takes the photos on their phone in the RAHTIS driver app, with no separate messaging apps or email. The app works in the driver's own language (including Finnish, Swedish, English, Estonian, Latvian, Lithuanian, Polish and Russian), so the same instructions work for the whole team. The instructions apply both to jobs for your own customers and to transports taken from the RAHTIS load board.

Step 1: Open the job and confirm arrival

The driver opens the task and presses Arrived at the delivery point. The arrival time and location are saved on the job with the same tap. In the Note on the equipment or load field, the driver briefly records what has been damaged and where, so there is no trying to remember the details in the evening.

Step 2: Take photos during the inspection and mark new damage

Under Inspection and photos, the driver photographs every side of the trailer or container, the seal and the load, taking extra photos if necessary. If the driver sees new damage, they mark it with the New damage option before taking the photo. The photo of the same side taken at collection is shown alongside, so an old dent is not accidentally recorded as new. Photos are taken with the app's Take photo button, so they are saved directly to the right job and stop. When photos are sent later by email or a messaging app, they easily end up on the wrong job or stay on the driver's phone.

Step 3: Proof of delivery and a final check before the stop is marked as done

Before pressing Mark as done, the driver can see the photos taken at that stop. If a photo is missing or unclear, it is retaken on the spot. As proof of delivery, the consignee signs on the screen along with their name, or the driver scans the signed consignment note. Once the stop is done, the photos, the note and the confirmation are visible to the haulier in the job details without any separate messaging.

What quality is required of damage photos?

A damage photo is not evidence if the damage cannot be seen in it. The insurer and the shipper compare the photos with the consignment note and other documents, and an unclear photo gives them grounds to dispute the claim.

Three photos: overall view, close-up, identifier

Take at least three photos. The first shows the whole damaged side, so the extent of the damage can be assessed. The second is a close-up of the damage, close enough to make out the crack, dent or tear. The third shows an identifier: the registration number, container number, trailer number or seal number, which ties the photo to this particular transport.

The most common quality problems: blur, glare, close-up only

Blur is the most common reason for an unusable photo. In a dim building, steady the phone or take the photo twice. Glare is another pitfall, especially on a container's sheet-metal surface: move to one side so that the sun or a lamp does not hide the damage. A close-up on its own, without an overall shot, leaves the location of the damage unclear.

The driver does not need to worry about image size: before sending, the app scales the photo down to about 1,600 pixels on the longer side. The damage and the seal number remain legible, but the file is many times lighter than the phone's original photo and goes through even on a slow connection.

Why does attaching a photo fail, and how do you fix it?

When a photo is not saved, the cause is usually one of these: camera access has been blocked, the phone's storage is full or the connection has dropped. They can usually be fixed on the phone in a few minutes.

Camera access

The RAHTIS driver app is a web app installed on the phone's home screen via the browser, not from an app store. If the driver has at some point denied camera access, allow it again in the browser's site settings: on Android, in the Chrome menu under Settings → Site settings → Camera; on iPhone, under Settings → Safari → Camera. Full storage also prevents a new photo from being taken, so delete old videos or downloads.

Updating the app

The app updates itself when it is opened with a network connection, so no separate update from an app store is needed. If the screen freezes, close the app and open it again. Do not log out if there are still unsent photos in the queue.

SymptomMost common causeFix
"No connection" at the top and photos are queuedMobile network has droppedCarry on working; the photos will be sent when the connection returns
The camera does not openCamera access blockedAllow the camera in the browser's site settings
No photo can be taken at allStorage fullFree up space on the phone
The screen does not updateThe app is stuck in an old stateClose and reopen the app while online

When the driver tells you what the screen says, the table usually leads you to the cause quickly.

What should you do if the signal is weak or photos will not upload?

Take the photos first; the queue takes care of sending

A weak signal does not stop you taking photos. Take all the photos you need in the app as normal. The app stores the entries and photos in a queue on the phone and sends them in the order they were made once the connection returns. The time of the tap goes with them, so a late upload does not change the recorded time of delivery. The top of the screen shows that there is no connection, and queued entries are marked.

If the signal is gone for a long time, you can drive on and let the queue clear once the lorry is back in coverage or on Wi-Fi. Tell drivers in advance that queued entries do not need to be redone and that there is no need to log in to the app again.

How to make sure the photos have arrived

Once the queue is empty and the connection notice has gone, the photos are on the server. The haulier can see them in the job details. If you are unsure, check the job in the office view before the driver deletes anything from the phone.

The handling of photos and other delivery documents is described in the RAHTIS terms of use and privacy notice.

Who sees the attached damage photos, and what happens to them?

Once the driver has photographed the damage, the haulier's dispatcher can see the photos in the job details as soon as they have been sent. The shipper who ordered the job sees the arrivals, confirmations, photos and locations in the transport tracking, so there is no need to ask for photos separately via a messaging app. The photos are saved on the job with the time and place they were taken, so it is clear afterwards at what stage the damage was recorded.

Photos as part of the proof of delivery

The damage photos are on the same job as the proof of delivery (POD) and the scanned consignment note. If a claim is made for the damage, the photos show what condition the goods were in at the moment of delivery. What is decisive, however, are the notes and reservations made on the consignment note or another document, so a photo supports the note but does not replace it.

What the dispatcher should do straight away

Open the job and check that the photos are sharp and the damaged area is visible. If photos are missing or unclear, contact the driver immediately, before the lorry has left the site. Notify the shipper of the damage without delay, so the claims procedure can start within the time limits.

How do damage photos differ from ordinary delivery photos?

An ordinary inspection photo and the proof of delivery document that the delivery took place: goods delivered, consignee signed, unit number visible. A damage photo documents a deviation: a dent, a break, a damp mark or a missing package. Both are on the same job, but they record different things.

An ordinary confirmation is enough when the delivery goes as it should. A damage photo must always be accompanied by a written note on the consignment note or a separate damage report, because a photo on its own does not show who was responsible when the damage occurred.

When the same delivery needs both

If damage to the goods is visible on unloading, the driver photographs it before the consignee signs for the delivery and records their reservations. The same job then holds the damage photos, the proof of delivery and the consignment note on which the damage has been noted. The delivery can be invoiced even while the damage is in dispute, and each party has its own evidence: you have the photos, the consignee has the reservation.

A practical rule for drivers: inspection photos are always taken; a damage entry is made only when something is out of the ordinary. Everything is saved to the same job, so later on nobody has to guess which photo belonged to which load.

FAQ

Can I attach damage photos afterwards, once the delivery has already been marked as done?

Photos should always be taken before the stop is marked as done. A photo sent later has weaker evidential value, because it does not show that the damage already existed at the moment of delivery. The statutory time limits also apply to the consignee's reservations: for apparent damage, they must be made no later than at delivery.

How many damage photos should be attached to a delivery?

An overall shot, a close-up of the damage and a photo of the identifier are usually enough. Extra photos can be taken if there are several areas of damage. Photograph the damage, not the whole load.

Does attaching photos work without a connection at the port?

Yes. Take the photos in the app as normal. They stay in a queue on the phone and are sent automatically when the connection returns, and the recorded time is the moment of the tap. Do not redo the entries, even if they appear in the queue.

Can I use the phone's own camera instead of the app?

It is not a good idea. Photos taken with the phone's camera stay in the gallery and have to be sent separately. They then easily end up on the wrong job or never get sent at all. A photo taken with the app is saved directly to the right stop with time and location.

What do I do if the driver sent the wrong photo?

Contact the driver immediately, before the lorry has left, and ask them to retake the correct photo in the app. Record this in the job's messages, so the shipper and the haulier see the same information.
